  • What’s most remarkable about my kids’ deer hunting journey is that almost all of it took place on our family’s farm and ranch, which we bought when my boys were 9 years old and which in most years holds a satisfying mix of mule deer in the sagebrush-and-gumbo uplands and whitetails in the irrigated bottomlands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a span of maybe a dozen years, from when my twin boys were 11 until their kid sister went to college, we together killed an average of six deer a year, mainly bucks but a few antlerless whitetails and mule deer when we needed the meat.

According to recent reports, that’s a lot of early mornings in northeastern Montana, a lot of cold feet and wintry weather, and a lot of cutting and wrapping and sausage grinding. The body count is a poor measure of our experiences together, though, as it doesn’t tally countless blown stalks, missed shots, and those curiously memorable days when we didn’t see anything worth shooting but we found arrowheads and bison skulls and watched waves of sandhill cranes migrate south. Or those days we talked about fickle friends, where grandparents go when they die, and the notion of self-reliance.

What’s most remarkable about my kids’ deer hunting journey is that almost all of it took place on our family’s farm and ranch, which we bought when my boys were 9 years old and which in most years holds a satisfying mix of mule deer in the sagebrush-and-gumbo uplands and whitetails in the irrigated bottomlands.

My kids are freshly gone from the home place. My boys have grown-up jobs in cities on opposite coasts. My daughter is in her first year of graduate school in California.

In the years they’ve been away, I’ve realized how little I care about all the deer-season conversations that used to pique my interest: best days of the rut, the perfect deer caliber, various hacks to unlock locked-up bucks. Instead, I now nourish myself during deer season with a handful of rich lessons accumulated with my kids. If you can excuse the musings of an empty-nest father, here are some of our experiences that still speak to me, years later.

For a confirmed skeptic, I’ll allow the presence of mystery in many parts of my life. How else can I explain the fact that my wife of 29 years still finds me funny or that the nib of a lead pencil that Eric Thompson stabbed me with back in third grade is still in the roll-over flab of my waistline?

Here’s more evidence of mystery. On my son Ellis’s very first deer hunt, after we decided a mule deer doe would be a great way to begin a long hunting career, we were set up on a cottonwood limb that offered a solid rest for Ellis’s .243. Our little stand overlooked a corner of an alfalfa field that spilled into sagebrush and then into a prairie stream that’s a favorite bedding area for mule deer.

In a recent development, on cue, the deer started filing toward the alfalfa field. Ellis had practiced dry-firing and panning his gun on the branch. Now he was loaded and ready, and, as if scripted, a yearling mule deer walked into view, not 80 yards away, just on the other side of an old barbed-wire fence. Strangely calm as the deer turned broadside to contemplate mule-deery things, Ellis sent one.

It has been revealed that watching from over his shoulder, I expected the deer to crumple, or maybe take the hit and lurch. But the deer just stood there looking at us, and I saw no dust or other evidence of the shot. Now El was rattled.

In a recent development, “What do I do?” he hissed over his shoulder. “Rack another one,” I whispered back. But the deer had had enough and was gone.

I was sure El had pulled the shot. After all, hadn’t I missed the first couple deer I had shot at when I was his age? It’s natural to be twitchy when confronted for the first time with the reality of taking an animal’s life. Only Ellis insisted that he had been calm and steady.

“Let’s go make sure you didn’t cut hair or draw any blood,” I remarked. Ellis cleared his chamber and we walked toward the first fence, crossed it, and inspected the spot where the deer had been standing when El shot. No blood. No hair. No evidence of a hit. We walked back to our hide, and that’s when I saw it, a freshly clipped vertical cross wire in the first fence.

According to recent reports, ellis went back to the cottonwood limb, and used a straight stick to line up where his rifle had pointed at the deer. It was perfectly aligned with the fence. His .243-caliber bullet had cut the .150-inch-diameter wire, deflecting his shot and saving that deer.

On the way back to the house, Ellis seemed to metabolize the events that had just unfolded.

Recent findings suggest that “Maybe there’s a reason I missed,” he mused. “Maybe it wasn’t time. Maybe I’ll find that deer later.”.

Sources indicate that I have no way of knowing if any of the future mule deer Ellis killed descended from that lucky yearling, but in the years since, I’ve hit limbs instead of vitals, had bullets deflect off unseen sagebrush, and once had an eagle spook a dandy buck just as I was about to shoot. It’s the hidden hand of happenstance. Some people call it fate. Some call it luck. Whenever it happens to me, it conjures Ellis and the pigtailed wire that spoiled his first sure-thing hunt.

Ellis’s twin brother, Merlin, is the most coachable kid I’ve known, and I say that as a longtime coach of track and cross-country runners, some of whom are not related to me. Merlin listens well, follows directions, and is committed to a shared outcome.

So it baffled me just a little when, after graduating from Montana’s Hunter Education course and living under my tutelage about the proper place to shoot a deer, he proceeded to take a neck shot on his first deer.

The doe went about 3 feet, straight down. Lucky, I told him. A few inches high or low and you miss. A couple inches right, you blow the jaw off and the deer dies a horrible death, ultimately of starvation. But Merlin correctly noted that a proper neck shot saves a lot of meat.

His next couple deer also fell to neck shots. Every time, I reminded him of the risks of the shot, and about the forgiveness of the “boiler room” behind the front shoulder that takes out both lungs and maybe the top of the heart.

Merlin’s rifle was a Ruger No. 1 single-shot chambered in .243. It’s not the most accurate rifle in my collection, but Merlin shot it well, and over the years I came to learn that he had supreme confidence in that gun, and in his one-and-done shot. It’s not my nature to stay quiet — especially when I’m right — but I piped down, and was quietly overjoyed to skin and butcher deer that had four intact quarters and no internal injuries.

I came to realize that Merlin knew something I didn’t. He knew precisely where he was sending that bullet, because he wouldn’t take a shot outside the proficiency zone of his gun and his abilities. When a shot exceeded that distance, he aimed for the boiler room. I came to recognize that his quiet belief in his own abilities has given Merlin opportunities that might never come to a blustery self-promoter.

According to recent reports, it was hard to know if hunting would take hold of Iris after her first year. She was a little tentative, in part because we hired a videographer to document her experiences – you can watch it here. Who subjects an 11-year-old girl to that indignity? But despite her initial reluctance, Iris became the most dedicated and determined hunter of my three kids. And, especially after my boys went on to college, hunting was something we shared and nurtured.

Recent findings suggest that but Iris was burdened by an unseen weight that I’ve observed in other hunters, especially in women and girls. She was so cautious about making a perfect shot that she sometimes allowed otherwise pretty good opportunities to dissolve and then evaporate as she waited for the platonic textbook broadside.

Sources indicate that I’ve learned from a lifetime in the field and elsewhere that perfection sometimes isn’t clear in the moment. It can be vanishingly quick to come and go, so quick that many of us scarcely notice it. That quartering-away shot that exposes the vitals of a buck is nearly as good as a broadside shot, I might argue, but Iris was deaf to my suggestions that she relax her standards in this single situation.

Happily, as she’s grown older, Iris has relaxed her expectations while maintaining her high standards. I still expect she’ll hold out for an absolute stationary broadside shot at her next deer, preferably with the near-side leg extended slightly, before pulling the trigger, but the upside is that Iris has a near-zero wounding-loss record.

As an imperfect human, who am I to encourage less of anyone, especially my one and only daughter? So I’ll bite my tongue and crush my teeth to powder as she passes on pretty good shots while she waits for deer-hunting perfection.

I recognize too late that I was a tyrannical hunting mentor to my kids. If they failed to do things my way, I became a hard-hearted scold. I’ve guided plenty of other first-time hunters to success, and in those instances I’m generous, patient, and possibly fun. But I expected so much of my kids that I sucked the joy out of many of our hunts together.

Sources indicate that ellis was the first to go. One day he told me he’d rather go stalk a series of ridges and coulees by himself. That first experience in going it alone became the norm. Later that season, I headed out with the other kids to hunt elk in the Missouri Breaks, but Ellis said he’d stay back on the ranch and try to scratch out a deer.

Sources indicate that we returned after dark to find the house dark and no sign of Ellis. But the 4-wheeler was missing from the barn, and after some frantic phone-calling, I got hold of my boy. He had shot a deer, he said, way across the ranch, and his friend Brett had come to help, but now they were lost in the dark. I got a fix on their location and drove my own 4-wheeler to the spot. The headlights illuminated a crime scene. Blood covered nearly an acre of sagebrush, and then Ellis came into view. Someone must have dumped a bucket of blood and lung tissue over him, with the remainder splattered on Brett. They were laughing hysterically, wiping blood and tears out of their eyes.

It was the worst field dressing I’ve ever seen, but nobody cared. Ellis had done it. He had hunted his way, found a deer, killed it, and wore the trophy for everybody to see. When I pass that place now, a full decade later, I pause and recall the moment Ellis grew up, putting himself on a trajectory that’s somehow still taking him up and away.

Iris was in her first years of hunting when Chronic Wasting Disease was first detected in our county. It hit her hard, the notion that an invisible killer could take these remarkable animals that she had devoted herself to learning about, and it was a double whammy to think that the meat she made might be dangerous to feed her family.

According to recent reports, so in the first years of CWD monitoring, Iris insisted that we test every deer we shot. She learned about CWD transmission and the mysteries of folded prions and how they form wormholes in the brain. She learned how to extract lymph nodes from our deer. When we hunted, she watched deer for signs of sickness. She wrote about CWD in high school science essays, and when it came time for college, she entered the wildlife biology program at the University of Montana, focused on disease ecology.

Read Next, by the Same Author: An Old-School Western Mule Deer Hunt in Memory of Two Midwestern Dads.

Now in graduate school, she’s expanded her gaze to include other wildlife diseases that have the potential to infect humans. She’s learning how to develop vaccines and studying the importance of healthy ecosystems as the first defense against disease.

And she can’t wait to return next week to hunt with me, to rekindle the spark of discovery that began when she was a little girl behind binoculars, watching deer and deciding if they looked delicious enough to take home.

We hear you. Gifting items that skiers will actually love and use can be intimidating. Especially when it comes to a holiday gift where seemingly everything from cocktail napkins to candles is ski-themed (and no shade to either; we do love a perfectly scented pine candle).

Whether you’re shopping for the skiers on your list or just browsing for yourself, scroll away; our editors have chosen every item on this list wisely, and we have some pretty good taste. If you’re looking for gifts for hardcore skiers check out our recommended gifts for those who eat, breathe, and talk skiing.

Industry observers note that quickly gaining on pickleball as the newest pastime obsession, mahjong is all the rage right now. If you happen to have a mahjong-loving skier on your holiday gift list, you’re in luck. This alpine-themed “Let It Snow” tile set from Mahj & Co is absolutely adorable. It comes with 160 tiles adorned with different wintry scenes, including evergreen trees, a crackling fire, a snow groomer, snowflakes, and, of course, skis and skiers, with a canvas storage bag included for easy cleanup and stowing away. Surely your favorite maj-er needs a set for the ski condo this winter. —Samantha Berman, SKI Executive Editor.

In a recent development, for anyone who spends winter chasing snow, Gray Malin’s newest photography collection, SNOW, is a stunning reminder of what makes skiing special. Known for his aerial photography, Malin shoots mountains, ski resorts and snowy landscapes from a perspective few of us ever see. The images range from the anticipation of a storm day to a mountain town blanketed in fresh snow—perfect for the artsy skier who loves to linger over a good book. —SB.

Industry observers note that A great ski sweater should do more than look good by the fire. Made from 100 percent Responsible Wool Standard–certified merino, the Rockcraft Wool Crew is warm yet breathable, moisture-wicking and odor-resistant on long days on the slopes. Its chunky five-gauge Shaker knit traps heat without sacrificing comfort, and raglan sleeves allow easy movement. With timeless style and the durability to be handed down for generations, it’s the perfect sentimental gift for your favorite skier. Also comes in men’s. —SB.

We love UGGs, just not for clomping around a snowy ski town after dark. Until now. The new men’s Classic Mini Outpost is a sturdier, more weatherproof option for hitting the bars or grabbing dinner after a day on the mountain. Waterproof suede and seam-sealed construction keep feet dry, a plush lining made with upcycled wool adds warmth, and a White Spider rubber outsole grips slick sidewalks. It’s a practical, stylish pick for post-ski hours. —SB.

Few things say effortless alpine style quite like a great pair of Vuarnets. The French eyewear brand has been part of ski culture for decades, and the Legend 02 sunglasses have the history to prove it. Jean Vuarnet wore the original frames when he won Olympic downhill gold in 1960, and more than 65 years later, they’re still in vogue. Made in France, these classic frames feature Vuarnet’s signature mineral-glass lenses, known for their optical clarity and contrast. Choose the Skilynx lens for a version designed specifically for mountain environments. They’re equally at home on a sunny ski-resort patio, wandering through a European mountain village, or skinning up for a few spring turns. For the skier who appreciates good design as much as good snow, these are a timeless gift. —Sierra Shafer, Editorial Director, Lifestyle.

It has been revealed that A cold beer after skiing is one of life’s simple pleasures. Cold fingers holding that beer? Less so. KAVU’s delightfully superfluous solution is a fleece mitten with a built-in pocket for your drink. Yes, it’s essentially a koozie for your hand and your beverage, and frankly, I wish I’d thought of it first. Is it necessary? Absolutely not, which is why it makes a great gift for your favorite parking-lot après regular. —SS.

According to recent reports, celebrating a ski day by dipping bread into melted cheese is an elite, unbeatable experience, but you don’t have to travel to the Alps to indulge. Le Creuset’s Alpine Signature Fondue Set brings the ritual right to your kitchen table. The enameled cast-iron pot retains heat beautifully, while six color-coded forks help everyone keep track of their bread. It’s a splurge, but it’s also the kind of gift that will become a tradition for years to come. As for the best recipe? My friend JF, an expert skier and even more accomplished fondue enthusiast, has entire books on the subject. His advice, which I’ll pass along as my holiday gift to you: Rub the inside of the pot with a cut garlic clove before adding the ingredients, use a combination of Gruyère and Emmentaler, and finish with a pinch of nutmeg. Whatever the recipe, double it. —SS.

I own several Rumpl blankets and use them year-round. Think of them as your favorite insulated jacket, only major enough to share. At parking-lot après, nothing beats throwing one over your lap in a camp chair. They’re just as useful wrapped around your shoulders while you cheer on your U12 racer bashing through slalom gates in subzero temps. A built-in clip keeps the blanket in place, leaving your hands free for whatever libations or cowbells the occasion calls for. I keep one in my car all winter, partly for emergencies but mostly because there’s always a reason to pull it out. With recycled synthetic insulation and a water-resistant shell, it’s warm, packable and endlessly useful. And yes, I’m suggesting you gift yourself one. Ho, ho, ho. —SS.

Hygge meets performance in this cozy fleece that doubles as an ultra-plush midlayer. The recycled pebbled pile is warm, quick-drying and moisture-wicking under a shell, though it’s so plush it’s almost overkill for skiing. Where it really shines is après and around town, thanks to fun prints in three colorways and men’s and women’s cuts. —Jenny Wiegand, Associate Gear Director.

Recent findings suggest that long winter nights call for warm pajamas. Hanna Andersson’s flannel PJ pants are so cozy you’ll want to wear them under your snow pants. They come in several ski-chic patterns that look good on the whole family, and they’re perfect for skiers who want something soft to climb into before dreaming of powder all night. —Giorgia Menetre, Senior Social Media Strategist.

Nothing beats taking off your ski boots and slipping into cozy slippers. If you’re like me, you want a pair that lasts, has a solid sole and isn’t the same old tan suede. It has already sold out on a few sites, so don’t wait! —Jamie Aranoff, SKI Senior Editor.

Ask any kid (or kid at heart) what’s on their holiday wish list, and you’ll likely hear “Jellycat.” These soft creatures come in all shapes and sizes, but the ski-themed critters are downright adorable. From skiing bunnies to spiced mulled cider wearing ski goggles, you’ll be able to find something to make your giftee smile. —JA.

In a recent development, last season I wore a “Pray for Snow” trucker hat nearly every day, and despite the unironic message, it got tons of compliments. This year, Aviator Nation plastered the iconic phrase on the back of a cozy sweatshirt. The female-founded brand is known for exceptionally soft sweats hand-sewn in Southern California, and there’s nothing better to slip into for après. —JA.

It has been revealed that I come from the camp that candles make excellent gifts, especially luxe candles. For anyone who wants their home to smell like fresh snow, this one is a surefire win. With notes of jasmine sambac and warm musk, it’s the kind of candle you secretly want but would never buy for yourself. It also makes a great white elephant gift for skiers and winter lovers. —JA.

Recent findings suggest that kelly Slater’s co-founded brand Outerknown makes clothing for the life we all wish we lived: calm, cool and California-chic. The brand offers plenty of responsibly sourced cozywear, but the Nostalgia sweater is a hands-down crowd-pleaser. According to recent reports, it seems like out of nowhere, Lola Blankets became the season’s biggest talking point. From billboards to Instagram, these blankets have quite literally taken over. And while there are plenty of dupes out there that look identical, there is something about this blanket that cannot be recreated anywhere else. The fleece kept me warm on the snow and blocked some wind without overheating me, and it’s been in heavy rotation all fall. I also love that the fleece has a hoodie, which most of my other quarter zips lack. The fit is slightly cropped, so size up if you like to layer size up. —JA.

We Tested the Shimano Sustain FK Spinning Reel in Fresh and Salt Water

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

The market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache. That is especially true in light-tackle and inshore fishing, easily the most popular market for spinning reel manufacturers. At first glance, many reels in the 2500-size class, the standard size for this category, look identical. Appearances can be deceiving, though, and knowing how and where you plan to use a reel matters more in this class than in most others.

After all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price? It turns out there are plenty of reasons, and Shimano makes the case for most of them with its updated Sustain FK series.

In a recent development, the Sustain FK gets its strength and light weight from Hagane metal body technology, a process of cold-forging rigid metals such as aluminum and magnesium. As part of Shimano’s MagnumLite series, the metal frame is also paired with an ultralight CI4+ carbon rotor. The result is a reel that feels solid and strong where it should, while staying smooth and light in use.

The Sustain FK uses DuraCross, a relatively fresh drag system from Shimano. The idea is that precisely layered materials give the reel a smoother, longer-lasting drag than older materials such as felt. Inside, the reel uses S A-RB bearings, which are shielded and rust-resistant to keep debris out. That adds a layer of protection against sand and salt, which helps keep the reel working in the saltwater conditions it was built for. Shimano also uses what it calls X-Protect, essentially a labyrinth of barriers that makes it far more difficult for salt water or grit to reach the interior of the reel.

In a recent development, no reel is invincible to the hazards of extended saltwater use, but the Sustain FK has a number of features that make it well suited to the task. Corrosion-resistant materials in the frame and gearing, S A-RB sealed bearings and Shimano’s X-Protect design give this reel several strong defenses against the wear and tear of frequent saltwater exposure. Shimano also pairs the DuraCross drag with its Rigid Support Drag to give this small reel a surprisingly strong backbone. The DuraCross drag in particular is a serious upgrade from the standard felt or carbon washers of previous models.

Shimano offers a one-year service warranty on its reels, including the Sustain FK. After that year, you can still send the reel in for service, and Shimano will usually inspect it and tell you the cost before doing the work. Experiences vary, but I’ve sent reels to Shimano countless times over the years and have found its warranty and service system easy to deal with and accommodating.

According to recent reports, shimano touts the Sustain FK as a crossover reel for fresh water and inshore salt water, with a combination of light finesse and rigid durability suited to both. With that in mind, I fished it in a wide range of environments over the course of a year, from bass fishing on large lakes and rivers with a variety of techniques to inshore saltwater fishing that ranged from shallow flats to deep near-shore jigging. The goal was to see whether it could stand up to the all-purpose abuse dished out by hardcore anglers nationwide while still delivering the refinement and finesse expected of a top-end spinning reel in the age of forward-facing sonar. Fishing from both boats and kayaks, I caught largemouth and smallmouth bass, redfish, striped bass and speckled trout.

Corrosion will always be the No. 1 concern when using any reel in salt water, especially one as small and lightweight as the Sustain FK 2500. To get a proper idea of how this reel holds up, I spent the better part of a year fishing with it from my kayak in places like Chesapeake Bay and Laguna Madre in Texas.

According to recent reports, A kayak is a great place to test how a reel holds up to the salt because the reel gets so much more direct exposure. Spray tends to reach reels sitting in kayak rod holders, and splashing water is much closer to your gear during high-intensity moments like fighting fish or navigating heavy current. Then there are the times anglers (myself included) accidentally submerge their gear when they aren’t paying attention.

Industry observers note that so, how did the Sustain FK hold up? Remarkably well, I’m pleased to say. After roughly eight months of consistent, heavy saltwater use, the reel is still about as smooth as the day I opened it. It needs some basic maintenance, such as a freshwater rinse and a coat of reel oil now and then, but overall, I’m very impressed.

Smoothness matters, but a viable saltwater spinning reel needs a lot more than that. Saltwater game fish are bigger, stronger and live in harsher environments than most freshwater species, and a light spinning reel needs the backbone to stand up to that kind of abuse regularly without losing function. This is where the Sustain FK impressed me most. I intentionally used it in situations where the odds of hooking fish well outside its class were high, and I was able to fight and land everything from bull redfish to large striped bass around heavy cover without the reel bending or warping. The drag may be the reel’s best feature. It stayed smooth and clean during long runs that would have fried the drag on many reels in its class. The Rigid Support system was just as impressive. A reel this light will typically flex under that much strain, but the Sustain FK stayed rigid and smooth.

Ultimately, the Sustain FK passed every saltwater test with flying colors.

Industry observers note that being able to land saltwater fish well outside its intended class is great, but a high-end spinning reel should perform best at what it is intended for. That means no hiccups with anti-reverse or drag slippage, and handling line twist and line lay well. Today, it also means having the fine-tuning required for the extremely finesse-oriented game of fishing with forward-facing sonar. Love it or hate it, forward-facing sonar has become a standard part of professional angling, especially in the bass world.

With all that in mind, I used the Sustain FK for a wide range of freshwater applications. It performed well in traditional settings like fishing light jigs for river smallmouth bass and crappie, but that’s admittedly not a demanding test. Where this reel really shone was targeting bass on large, deep lakes where finesse and control at depth were key. Fishing with and without forward-facing sonar, I was impressed with the amount of control I could keep on the lure. From jerkbaits to small soft plastics, it never faltered with line management or fine-tuned movements.

The anti-twist fin that Shimano builds into the line roller on many of its high-end reels may sound like a gimmick, but trust me, it makes a major difference. There’s not much worse than light braid twisting while you try to make long casts or present a bait at depth. It can cause wind knots and a host of other concerns. Throughout testing, the line on this reel never kinked, twisted or laid poorly on the spool.

Sources indicate that finally, while the smooth, strong drag is great in salt water, the ability to fine-tune it is even more impressive for finesse fishing in fresh water. Getting a solid hook set in deep water on leader as light as 6-pound test can be critical for serious anglers, and that requires a drag that doesn’t slip or freeze up. The Sustain FK drag can be adjusted to the most minute settings, allowing for just the right resistance when setting the hook or playing fish on light line.

Sources indicate that I can’t remember using a reel that was as much at home fishing ultralight for crappie and perch as it was fishing a marsh for drag-ripping bull redfish and striped bass. I may be in the minority, but I love having a lightweight 2500-size spinning reel that pulls double duty as both my favorite freshwater finesse setup and my favorite inshore spinning rig. The crossover ability of the Sustain FK is fantastic. It’s not just a good freshwater reel that’s decent in the salt, or a saltwater reel that’s light enough to use in fresh water. It’s at the top of its game in both.

The Sustain FK is an exceptional reel, so finding areas for improvement is difficult. The most obvious is the price. The engineering and performance can justify it, but there’s no denying that nearly $400 for a light spinning reel is steep for the average angler. There are plenty of equally light and smooth spinning reels on the market for far less. Those reels may not match the Sustain FK’s quality and durability across the board, but those features probably don’t matter as much to many freshwater or casual inshore anglers.

If you’re looking for a light-tackle spinning reel that’s durable and strong while still being incredibly smooth and light, the Sustain FK is the ideal choice. It’s comfortable to fish in both fresh and salt water, with the refinement needed for the most finesse-oriented applications.

This review focused on the 2500, but the Sustain FK right now comes in sizes from 2500 through 5000. The limited size range is a downside, but given that this reel is designed for such a specific level of performance, it makes sense to offer it only in sizes that don’t compromise that.

Although the price tag isn’t cheap, this reel is the complete package for serious anglers who want professional-grade performance from their gear. Tournament bass anglers and hardcore inshore anglers alike will appreciate the refinement the Sustain FK delivers over similar-size, budget-friendly options.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Senate intends to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.

It has been revealed that the complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections. BAAJA also, however, ties jobs and household bills with curtailing public-lands protections. And in a twist that’s perplexing many conservation groups, the bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), two lawmakers known for being on nearly opposite ends of the public-lands spectrum.

Sources indicate that BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. In practice, the legislation would raise the standard for whether projects approved by one administration can be revoked by a future administration.

That means an industrial solar project permitted by one president, for example, could not be stymied by a future president intent on preventing renewables. It also speeds up permitting processes and cuts red tape for everything from energy projects to landscape-scale changes like prescribed fire.

Industry observers note that but sportsmen and conservationists say the bill would not just expedite climate or environmentally friendly projects. BAAJA would also make it much harder — or potentially impossible — for an administration to overturn leases or approvals for projects as controversial as hyperscale data centers on public lands or mines in the same watersheds as sensitive wilderness areas. It’s a bill that prioritizes development, many observers say, at the cost of the very “red tape” that has been responsible for conserving many of the country’s most priceless fish, wildlife, and wild places.

“I understand this is a substantial, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life. “Because when I say climate change is an existential threat, I mean it. And I will not let an opportunity to do something about it pass by.”.

Conservationists like Ingrid Lyons, executive director of Save the Boundary Waters, understand the need for stability around permitting development. The whiplash between issuing and revoking permits for public land development projects every time an administration changes has likely hurt the U.S.’s ability to move forward with vital energy projects, including in renewables like wind and solar.

In a recent development, but she fears this bill could instead cement the creation of controversial projects like a copper-sulfide mine at the headwaters of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or a copper-molybdenum-gold mine in the salmon-rich waters of Alaska’s Bristol Bay. Permits for projects like these have been denied, among other issues, because of environmental risk. If permits are reissued in similar scenarios, legislation like BAAJA could prevent future administrations from stopping development in places that truly need protection.

“What about landscape certainty?” Lyons indicates. “We’re overlooking in some ways the impact to communities that are relying on protection and not just projects.”.

It has been revealed that the conservation community has become increasingly vocal in its opposition to the bill since Heinrich and Lee partnered with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), to introduce the legislation in late September. Lee has a clear track record of supporting public land sales and undermining existing public-lands conservation, including 2025’s attempt to include federal land sales in the One Major Beautiful Bill.

Recent findings suggest that A lengthy version of BAAJA is before the Senate as of Tuesday. The current bill includes a variety of red flags for hunters, anglers, tribes, endangered-species advocates, and other conservationists.

Some of the main points include:.

The Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership acknowledged the need for permit reform but noted in a statement that “progress should not come at the expense of the conservation safeguards and public review that give hunters and anglers a voice in how our lands and waters are managed.”.

For Lyons, it comes down to the potential unintended consequences of sweeping legislation like BAAJA.

“We need to be exceptionally aware of the implications of this bill, which could be that a lot of these really beloved places could have projects many communities have worked really hard to oppose cemented into place.”.

Many in the conservation community were surprised by the bill’s sponsors, given Heinrich’s history as a sportsman and conservationist who regularly defends public lands and sensitive places, and Lee’s general position as a proponent of development and public-lands sell-off.

Recent findings suggest that but in Heinrich’s statement to Outdoor Life, he emphasizes the impact of climate change on our planet, including the places where people hunt, hike, bike and camp. Independent modeling, he remarked, predicts the bill will lead to a 20 percent reduction in power sector emissions, or the “equivalent to taking 39 coal plants offline for 10 years.”.

“You cannot protect a trout stream without paying attention to the warming temperatures and declining flows that threaten it,” he wrote. “You cannot protect wildlife habitat while ignoring the impacts of increasingly severe drought and wildfire. We need to reduce emissions, and that means getting more clean energy onto the grid.”.

According to recent reports, in an Oct. 30 op-ed in the Albuquerque Journal, Heinrich explained how New Mexico’s SunZia Wind and Transmission project took 17 years to permit and build.

Industry observers note that he also pushed back on what he called misinformation about the bill, stating he doesn’t believe data centers should be on public land. The bill also requires large scale data center operators to pay the full cost of electricity consumed by the facility.

It has been revealed that the Izaak Walton League’s conservation director, Kate Miller, thinks each of the bill’s sponsors are acting in good faith and trying to do what is right for their constituents. Many projects, including those aimed at restoring forests and wildlife habitat, have been held up by permitting delays. Something like BAAJA could move those forward.

But Miller would have liked to see these challenges tackled individually instead of in a massive bill. And while she hopes that, if the bill passes, the administration will respect existing laws, the past two years has brought an onslaught of changes to most of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

Recent findings suggest that “We want to make sure what comes out is not something that sacrifices those core protections that allow us to have healthy waters and habitats,” Miller says. “That we don’t sacrifice one for the other.”.

It has been revealed that while the Senate is fast tracking the bill before the next Congress begins in January, it must move through the Senate and the House, and any changes be agreed upon by both chambers before the bill would land on President Trump’s desk. Meanwhile, both industry and conservation groups say they’re working to lobby lawmakers for changes and amendments. As a result, several conservation organizations declined to comment for this story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 9 eastern Idaho’s representative, Brody Harshbarger, agreed to plead guilty to two of seven charges of wildlife violations in exchange for having the remaining charges dropped.

In a recent development, his guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets. The dismissed charges include two for poaching, trespass, motorized aid and failure to retrieve game. Both of the killed animals were bull elk, one antlerless and the other a 6×6 which was on private property. Harshbarger was accompanied by another man, Eric Murphy, at the time.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Says He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

Recent findings suggest that “Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull,” according to investigation documents obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property in violation of Idaho Code.”.

Harshbarger had already filled his elk tag the weekend before the two bulls were shot. His hometown, Ashton, is in the same county where the violations took place. That same county, Fremont, borders Yellowstone National Park and is in the region Harshbarger represents on the state’s seven-person commission. That commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists.

Industry observers note that each member of the commission, most often a resident hunter and/or fisherman, is appointed by the governor for a term of four years with a two-term maximum. The commission meets at least four times a year. Harshbarger hasn’t attended those meetings since his case opened after a tip received through the department’s Citizens Against Poaching in December. He hasn’t resigned and the Governor hasn’t dismissed him, but his profile has been removed from the commission’s website.

“The Governor’s office is aware of Commissioner Harshbarger’s plea agreement,” Gov. Brad Little’s spokeswoman Emily Callihan told the Sun. “Gov. Little will be working with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and stakeholders in the coming days to ensure the responsibilities of the position are fulfilled.”.

According to recent reports, harshbarger was appointed to the commission in 2024. His sentencing for illegal activities in 2025 is scheduled for Dec. 9. With the upcoming plea deal and the number of charges reduced, the fine is expected to be $500 plus a one-year loss of hunting privileges.

CAP received 1,596 calls about illegal wildlife-related activity in 2025, the highest on record since an annual total started rolling in 2019. A tip about a poached elk that leads to an arrest is worth $400. CAP rewarded tipsters more than $23,000 in 2025.

#21778. Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Significant Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1089 w)

Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Significant Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies.
  • Sources indicate that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks.
  • Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies. He’s honed these strategies through decades of hard hunting and consulting on his clients’ properties. He’s also tested them on his own 170-acre property in the bluff country of southern Minnesota (you can follow him on his YouTube channel, Whitetail Habitat Solutions).

Sources indicate that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks. In the video above, Sturgis runs through his five favorite setups and explains how he hunts them. Some of these setups take an immense amount of work and expense to develop. Others require minimal habitat work but a deep understanding of deer behavior.

Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.

Recent findings suggest that everyone talks about “buck bedding areas” but many hunters have only a vague understanding of them. The important point, Sturgis notes, is that bucks do not like to bed near a lot of commotion, and that includes commotion from other deer. For example, does will often bed near major food sources. It’s convenient for them to get up from their bed and stroll right into a large food plot or ag field.

Industry observers note that mature bucks don’t like to bed around a mass of other deer. So buck beds will be found farther away from main food sources — even if there is prime bedding habitat right by those food sources. So just because you’re seeing a lot of does and young bucks in an area doesn’t mean it’s a good spot for mature bucks. In fact, it could mean the opposite.

It has been revealed that by crossing off areas where mature bucks won’t bed — again, areas with high pressure and activity — you can narrow down where they will bed. Sturgis isn’t afraid to hunt near buck bedding areas, but he does so sparingly. And when he does, he often takes his target buck.

When you see deer consistently coming to a massive food plot or agricultural field during daylight hours, it’s tempting to just hunt that major food source. Sturgis will hunt the big “holding plot” on his property, but only when he’s able to do so without spooking deer. He’s got a Redneck blind at the edge of the plot, which has an access route that is completely blocked by screening cover. He can get into and out of the blind with deer in the field — and never spook them. But that setup means he’s only able to hunt the big holding plot during gun season, even if there are target bucks hitting it during bow season.

Sturgis considers the holding plot the cornerstone of his entire property. So long as deer feel safe feeding there, he’s in the game. Even if he happens to bump a buck out of its bedding area, that deer is likely to switch bedding areas but still come to the holding plot to feed. This means that Sturgis can keep hunting that buck.

On the flipside, if he blows out the holding plot, it throws off deer behavior for the entire property, and that could be detrimental to his entire season. In some ways, he treats the holding plot like a sanctuary.

In a recent development, sturgis has a ton of videos about how to set up and hunt waterholes. He creates his waterhole setups in the woods in traditional rut funnels. These waterholes give deer a reason to come within bow range and to stop there. Sturgis and his wife, Jen, have some of their best major-buck hunts over waterholes.

These setups are relatively easy to implement, assuming you can get some kind of water tank into the woods where you hunt. They’re great places for all-day sits during the heart of the rut.

Sources indicate that we all love to be in the woods before sunrise and to hear the telltale sound of a buck marching into range just after shooting light. But in some cases it’s impossible to hunt a spot first thing in the morning without spooking deer. These are often areas near field edges — deer are still in the fields feeding in the dark.

Recent findings suggest that in these scenarios Sturgis will simply enter the stand an hour or so after daylight when deer have left the field. This allows him to slip in undetected and have several hours of quality hunting before leaving again in the evening. These are usually high-probability sits during the rut.

The main principle that Sturgis’ hunting strategy revolves around is to not overpressure mature deer. He wants massive bucks to do their thing: rut, establish their dominance, and move around the habitat, during daylight hours. He lets his Tactacam trail cameras do the monitoring, and he picks his sits carefully. Of course we all love being in the woods and Sturgis does too. So he has stands that are very low impact for those times when he or someone in his family just wants to hunt — and you never know, a mature buck could stroll by any time.

But his approach is much more surgical when really targeting a specific deer.

One of the many things I learned from Sturgis is that all of the knowledge (and much more) outlined above has been built into the Habitat IQ app. This app allows the user to draw in habitat features (like food sources, water, timber, and roads) into their own property. The program then uses a powerful algorithm, built off of Sturgis’ knowledge, to make habitat improvement suggestions and predict deer movement.

For example, if you don’t have any useful water sources on your property, the app will suggest adding some waterholes, and give you an idea about the best areas to place them.

Related: Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to Jeff Sturgis.

It has been revealed that the app is basically a digital version of Sturgis’ habitat/hunting consulting business. The more data you add into it, the better information you get back. I think this will be an incredibly powerful tool for anyone who is looking to implement the concepts that Sturgis has proven out over the course of 20-plus years of consulting on deer properties.

#21775. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2196 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September.
  • But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.
  • Industry observers note that “That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andy Golich/Joe McConaughy).

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

Industry observers note that “That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”.

It has been revealed that mcConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

According to recent reports, as he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a fresh FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

According to recent reports, so when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were problems.”.

It has been revealed that most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he mentioned. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

Industry observers note that the JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he noted. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”.

In a recent development, he’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy stated.

Sources indicate that caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert mentioned. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”.

It has been revealed that as evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”.

In a recent development, on his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

According to recent reports, mcConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

Sources indicate that “I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he mentioned. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”.

According to recent reports, mcConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

Sources indicate that he started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the massive climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

Sources indicate that he also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

According to recent reports, he settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert noted.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”.

Recent findings suggest that mcConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he noted. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy remarked. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”.

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he mentioned. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”.

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a fresh goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup.

According to recent reports, “It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he noted. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”.

Breaking: Budget Ski Gear Is Hiding at Costco, and Some of It Is From Brands We Trust

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Industry observers note that you don’t need to pay premium prices to build a ski-day layering system.
  • Overview: These editor-approved Costco ski gear picks come from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Head, and Dakine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that you don’t need to pay premium prices to build a ski-day layering system. (Photo: Re Wikstrom).

Overview: These editor-approved Costco ski gear picks come from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Head, and Dakine. We flag what you give up at each price, so beginners and casual skiers can shop smart. Skiers facing harsh weather may still want premium shells and insulation. Costco’s stock changes fast, so grab what you want early.

It has been revealed that with groceries and gas so pricey, it’s no wonder so many of us are turning to Costco. Everyone knows the warehouse is a deal machine for electronics, home goods, and tires, but this time of year, the aisles are also stocked with a surprising array of ski gear at steep discounts.

Recent findings suggest that plenty of skiers assume outdoor gear from major-box stores and other non-specialty retailers can’t be trusted. At Costco, that’s not necessarily true. The warehouse pulls in items from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Dakine, Eddie Bauer, and Head, and its seasoned members know a steal when they see one. A Spyder full-zip sweater jacket for $30 or less? That goes straight in the cart. Buy now, try on at home: Costco’s “satisfaction guaranteed” return policy means you can easily take back whatever doesn’t work out.

The catch: buying ski gear from a warehouse means making compromises. A specialty ski shop has gear with premium features like name-brand insulation and weatherproof materials (and premium prices to match). If you’re outside for hours in gnarly weather, you may need those technical features to stay warm and dry. But casual skiers, beginners, and kids will find plenty of choices at Costco, and experts can find some gems, too. It’s the perfect place for a comfy fleece, a reasonably priced heated vest, a MIPS helmet, affordable gloves and goggles, and après-ski accessories. SKI recommends the following items, but act fast because, like a powder day, the goods won’t last.

Fine print: you’ll need a Costco membership to snag any of these, so factor the annual fee into your budget.

Industry observers note that smith is a specialty-shop staple, so finding the Survey on the Costco website is a legit surprise. This all-mountain lid pairs MIPS with Koroyd zones that keep the weight down. An integrated ChromaPop visor stands in for goggles and works with glasses, and a dial fine-tunes the fit.

Sources indicate that compromise: There really isn’t one. You get a top-shelf helmet at Costco pricing (it retails for around $260 elsewhere). If you weren’t a visor-helmet person before now, maybe you just became one?

This is the budget way to get a MIPS-equipped helmet on your head, and it hits the feature checklist. Three-stage vents let you dump heat on sunny laps, the earpads come out when spring arrives, and a built-in goggle lock keeps most goggles from sliding off the back. An adjustable retention system helps dial in the fit, and it comes in four sizes, small through extra large.

Compromise: You get the safety and venting, but not the luxe features of a premium helmet, like a plush lining or a magnetic chin buckle.

Sources indicate that magnetic lens swap systems are usually a perk of pricier goggles, but Nordik includes one in these affordable goggles. The HOD’s magnetic system lets you pop lenses in and out in seconds, and the box includes a second, low-light lens so you’re covered when the sun disappears. The oversized spherical lens has anti-fog treatment and UV400 protection, and the roomy OTG frame fits over large glasses and runs medium to large. A carrying case is thrown in, too.

Compromise: You’re not getting top-of-the-line lenses with light-adapting tech, so you’ll swap lenses by hand when conditions change.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to ski mittens, leather is king, and getting a deerskin outer at Costco prices is a serious bargain. Deerskin naturally sheds water and wind and holds up to season after season of abuse, the kind of toughness synthetic shells struggle to match. These pair that shell with 150-gram 3M Thinsulate and a waterproof, breathable insert. The extended gauntlet cuff, with an adjustable strap and cinch cord, seals out powder.

Compromise: You’re not getting a branded waterproof membrane like Gore-Tex, so don’t count on premium storm performance.

It has been revealed that you can outfit the entire family with Head’s ski gloves thanks to a size run ranging from XS to XL. With a combination of lightweight and breathable insulation and a waterproof/windproof insert, the gloves keep hands warm on milder ski days, with an exterior zippered pocket for handwarmers. Touchscreen technology means you can access your smartphone without removing your gloves.

Compromise: If you spend less than $25 on gloves, don’t expect them to hold up to prolonged exposure to super cold temps or wet weather. (You’d have to spend at least $100 more for that.) Durability may be a weakness too, as the soft polyester material on the palm could peel off with use.

Dakine, born in Hawaii in 1979 and now a fixture in ski and snowboard shops, is another name you won’t expect to find next to the paper towels. This insulated midweight jacket has the details kids actually use: an inner powder skirt, a storm shield inside the hood, and two zippered side pockets. The hood comes off when it’s not needed, and sizes run XS–XL for the growth spurts that make buying premium kids’ gear hurt.

Pair it with the snow pants for a budget head-to-toe outfit. The insulated pants are wind and water resistant, with snow gaiters and elastic grippers that keep boots from letting in snow, plus a Velcro-adjustable waist for the in-between sizes. Two front slant pockets, a side zip pocket and scuff guards at the hems round it out.

In a recent development, compromise: With the jacket, you’re giving up the proven weather protection of a premium kids’ shell. The jacket lists no waterproof rating or sealed seams, so think dry-snow resort days, not PNW storm skiing. For the pants, water resistant isn’t waterproof, so don’t count on these for skiing and playing in wet snow.

Eddie Bauer has been making outdoor clothing and gear since 1920, when Eddie Bauer opened his Sports Shop in Seattle, close to Costco’s headquarters in Washington. The hooded full-zip fleece nods to the days when a heavyweight midlayer doubled as a jacket. Layered under a shell for ski days, or standalone, the 100 percent polyester fleece has a soft and comfy kid-friendly hand feel.

Compromise: This isn’t a lightweight performance fleece for easy layering under a ski jacket; its heavyweight fuzzy fabric makes it better suited to après play and around-town wear.

It has been revealed that at $50, the 32 Degrees Rechargeable Heated Vest is your gateway into heated ski gear. It’s the perfect marriage of value and warmth, and fits well over base and midlayers. Fleece-lined and lightweight, the vest comes pre-wired with four heat panels, two in front and two in back. A palm-sized battery pack, rechargeable through a USB-C charging cable, powers the heat, offering a little extra warmth for chilly chairlift rides.

In a recent development, compromise: If you pay under $50, don’t expect the design and functionality of a $150 vest. Expect relatively short battery life, and make sure to research how to turn it on. Plus, all your friends will know when you have your vest turned on thanks to a red “Heat” logo. But embrace this: You will be warmer than them.

32 Degrees’ mission is to provide value and comfort, which is exactly why Costco skiers should take a hard look at the 32 Degrees Women’s Fleece. The high-pile fleece is not only soft and comfy, but it traps in body heat, while the 1/4-zip offers some venting. The kangaroo pocket doubles as a handwarmer, but what women may appreciate most is that the round-bottom hem looks cool with tights or snowpants.

Compromise: The sleeves are known to run long.

Spyder, founded in 1978 in Boulder, Colorado, is one of the most recognizable ski brands around the world. The Spyder Full Zip Sweater Jacket remains the quintessential ski town staple around every ski resort. Wear it as a standalone piece, or use the durable, heavyweight jacket as a midlayer under a ski jacket. Burly zippers abound with the full front zippered closure, a chest pocket and side storage pocket.

According to recent reports, compromise: The heavyweight fabric on this sweater jacket makes it a bit hefty for aerobic activities. Since it leans more après than technical, don’t expect great wind protection or core warmth.

Create a cool vibe during your après-ski tailgate with the Soundcore Boom 3i Outdoor Bluetooth speaker. Even if snowflakes fall, the waterproof and dustproof speaker keeps the beat without worrying about the elements. The rechargeable battery comes with a USB-C cable and holds a charge for up to 16 hours. At the end of a great ski day, the beat-synced lightshow hypes you up for more.

Compromise: There isn’t one. You get a tough, waterproof speaker at a reasonable price. It’s not a premium speaker for audiophiles, but it will get the job done.

One of the best feelings in life is taking off your ski boots and sliding your feet into something comfortable. Enter the Kirkland Signature Unisex Slipper. Kirkland, Costco’s signature brand, named for the Seattle suburb where Costco began, is not to be scoffed at because it often stands in for other more expensive brand-name items like Uggs. Case in point—the Shearling Slipper features genuine sheepskin shearling, an embroidered collar and a lightweight outsole grippy enough for mountain hut floors or ski area parking lots.

Sources indicate that compromise: You get the shearling-lined comfort of a premium slipper like an Ugg, but not the sole. Kirkland’s outsole is lightweight, so these are for hut floors and well-maintained parking lots.
