The Burris Buck: How I Tagged the Biggest Mule Deer of All Time

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this story, “Greatest Mule Deer of Them All,” appeared in the December 1975 matter of Outdoor Life.
  • According to recent reports, I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me.
  • According to recent reports, when I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this story, “Greatest Mule Deer of Them All,” appeared in the December 1975 matter of Outdoor Life. Burris’ buck remains, all these years later, the No. 1 typical mule deer buck ever taken by a hunter, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. The antlers are now owned by Cabela’s. Burris tagged the buck on Oct. 19, 1972 in Dolores County, Colorado.

According to recent reports, I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me. Till then I’d figured on stillhunting to a plateau covered with scattered oak brush 400 yards north of me. A clump of brush there would have been a fine place to take a stand.

According to recent reports, when I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run. I was almost on the plateau when I noticed movement in the oak brush and aspens on the other side of the canyon. I slammed to a stop and stared at the biggest deer I had ever seen. His body was enormous, and his rack seemed large enough for an elk.

Industry observers note that he wasn’t running flat out, but I knew I had to shoot in a hurry. The range was about 250 yards. The buck was moving up the canyon and away from me when I found him in my Leupold 3X-to-9X scope, I put the crosshairs on his back and touched off my Sako .264. He went down in his tracks. My substantial-game handloads consist of 125-grain Nosler bullets backed with 66.5 grains of No. 4831 powder. It’s a very potent load.

Related: My First Buck Was the Biggest Typical Mule Deer Ever Taken with a Bow. I Almost Discarded the Antlers.

In a recent development, I watched him for a while to make sure he wasn’t going to get up, and then I ran down a side canyon and up the other side of the substantial one to the fallen buck. When I ran my hands over the huge 18-point rack, I knew the antlers were very good. I was sure the deer would score high in the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book.

According to recent reports, if someone could have told me that my 1969 Colorado buck wasn’t even good enough to make the minimum score for listing in the record book, I wouldn’t have believed him. That’s the way it turned out, but a still bigger deer was ranging the same stretch of country.

Sources indicate that I’m 37. My wife and I live in Seguin, Texas, with our 17-year-old son and two daughters, aged 15 and eight. I’m a construction superintendent with an outfit that builds shopping centers, high-rise office buildings, and similar units.

Except for 3½ years spent in the U.S. Air Force, I’ve lived in Texas all my life. I began hunting when I was seven. My dad got me started and taught me to be a good hunter. I killed my first Texas whitetail when I was 13, and I’ve been nuts about deer hunting ever since. Though many of our Texas deer are so small we call them jackrabbits, we do have some large whitetails in the southern brush country. Some of those bucks field-dress at 200 pounds or a bit more, and some have exceptional antlers. Many years of hunting brush-country deer gave me trophy-hunting fever.

I have always wanted to hunt Dall or Stone sheep in Alaska or British Columbia, but I’ve never had the money or the time. I finally decided that the next-best thing was to stay with deer and hunt trophy antlers.

My interest in camping had a lot to do with that first mule-deer hunt in Colorado in 1969. My friends and I have several four-wheel-drive vehicles and an assortment of camping gear. Charlie Fuller of Floresville, and Jack Smith of San Antonio, do a lot of hunting with me. Jack is my age. He’s a carpenter. Charlie, a few years younger, has a fertilizer-application operation. Both like to hunt deer the way I do, and they like to camp. Early in 1969 we decided to hunt in the mountains where we could camp on public land and do without guides and outfitters. We call it a “poor-boy hunt.”.

In a recent development, I did quite a bit of research on trophy mule deer before we chose the San Juan National Forest. From what I’d read in Outdoor Life and other outdoor magazines, I knew that many giant bucks were taken not too far from the Four Corners, where Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado touch.

In a recent development, I also bought a copy of the 1964 edition of the Boone and Crockett Club’s book, Records of North American Massive Game. Study of the section on mule-deer trophies backed up my contention that southwestern Colorado would be a good place to go. We knew there were better bets, such as the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in Upcoming Mexico, but we couldn’t get permits, and we wanted to go into country where we could camp on public land. We eventually drove to Cortez, Colorado, and hunted northeast of town.

Recent findings suggest that the three of us all got bucks that first year, and my massive buck had a rack that measured 41 inches across the outside spread. Each antler had “cheater” points extending horizontally from the outside curves of the main beams. Though the rack had a very unusual spread, the tines weren’t very long, and that’s why my trophy didn’t make the record book.

When I killed the deer, I didn’t know much about official scoring systems for big game, but I did know that where there was one grandote (a Mexican term we use for big bucks) there should be more. We didn’t need a better reason to head back into the same area. We’ve never been sorry.

It has been revealed that the second year, I got a buck with a 33-inch outside spread. The third year, I was lucky enough to come up with another good deer. Every season I’ve hunted in those mountains, except one, I’ve taken a buck with an outside antler spread of 30 inches or better, and other members of my party have taken very good bucks too. Many hunters in the area kill deer with spreads as narrow as 12 inches. Every fall I pass up many deer to get the best one I can find.

Most of the men in our group hunt that way. We all love the mountains, and we like to hunt hard from dawn to dark. We don’t want to miss one minute of hunting on these trips. None of us will take a small buck unless time is running out on the last day.

I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too. I’m usually the cook because I enjoy it. We come into camp each evening, warm up by our wood stove in the cooktent, swap stories about what happened during the day, and take our time over meals while we proposal the next day’s hunt. Then we sack out early enough for a good rest so that we can do it all over again.

It has been revealed that we go back into the Cortez area each year because it has proved itself, and because our camping gear is suited to that kind of country. We’re not equipped to backpack into remote areas or pack in with horses.

Sources indicate that our cooktent, which also serves as a community area, is a 14 x 16-foot wall tent. We have 9 x 12 Coleman sleeping tents. Everybody contributes something to our outfit. We found out during our first trip that it’s best to take plenty of blankets and raingear.

On the front end of our trailer is mounted a large box in which we pack all our food and some other items. If the weather is warm during our hunt, we have all our venison butchered, wrapped, and quick-frozen in Cortez. We pack the meat and dry ice in the box for our trip home. If the weather is cold, we hang our field-dressed deer from a game pole and then haul them home whole for butchering there. Either way, the venison we put in our freezers provides delicious meals far into the winter.

We make our trips from Texas to Colorado with two 4WD’s. The big unit is my three-quarter-ton Dodge Power Wagon equipped with a winch. Behind the Dodge we tow a Jeep on a 20-foot trailer. We usually ride in the wagon and pack the Jeep and the trailer with gear.

Our average cost per man totals about $155, and that includes Colorado’s nonresident deer license ($50). A massive chunk of the rest of each man’s expenses goes for gas. We drive straight through from Texas. That takes 20 to 24 hours, depending on driving conditions. We use the Jeep each day to put men out in hunting areas, so we burn a lot of gas. We bring plenty of steaks and a normal supply of groceries such as beans, potatoes, flour, canned goods, breakfast mixes.

I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too.

According to recent reports, we plan to arrive in our hunting area the Thursday before the Saturday opener of the deer season, which is always in late October. It takes two days to set up camp, get organized, and do a little scouting. We figure on hunting three to five days, but we do not set up a hard-and-fast schedule.

According to recent reports, as few as two men have gone to Colorado with me and as many as eight, but everything seems to go along smoothest with about four in the party. In 1972, the year I shot the world-record mule deer, there were four of us. Jack Smith went along, but Charlie Fuller couldn’t get away. Robbie Roe and Bruce Winters were my other partners. I knew them through my job, and we had done a lot of hunting together.

It has been revealed that we drove up into Colorado and camped in the same spot I’d picked out four years earlier. I knew the hunting country fairly well by that time, and I had selected five specific areas that seemed to hold the most deer and the biggest bucks. They’re all laced with relatively thick oak brush, some aspens, and a few pines. Thick oak brush is the key to success. If you’ve got tangles of that stuff and lots of them, you’re going to find deer.

According to recent reports, the oak-brush areas most attractive to deer run to broken terrain in the form of canyons and side canyons, plateaus, and mesas. The best technique for hunting that kind of terrain is a combination of stillhunting and standing. I like to stillhunt the plateaus and small canyons. I’ve learned that deer work the small finger canyons and get down into the very bottoms of them. They range back and forth through the canyons, often go up on the mesas and plateaus.

That’s why the combination of hunting techniques works so well. When I’m stillhunting I often spot deer ahead of me or across a canyon or draw. If I take a stand on a good vantage point I may have deer working toward me.

The problem is that deer may use one area today and vacate it tomorrow. So I choose an area and hunt it out. If deer are there, I stick with it; if they aren’t I move to the next area. That isn’t hard to do, because the San Juan country is mostly rolling terrain, and the altitude is only about 8,500 feet where we hunt.

Our first day of hunting in 1972 began in typical fashion. We checked the wind direction before dawn and decided on the areas each man would hunt. Then we piled into the Jeep and headed up a mountain two-track. I dropped Robbie off first and then Bruce. A few miles farther on, Jack got out of the vehicle. Dawn wasn’t much more than a dull-gray promise in the eastern sky. The black void above us was spitting drizzle.

“Robbie and Bruce will walk back to camp whenever they feel like it,” I told Jack. “You want me to pick you up at a set time, or do you want to hunt all day in the rain?”.

“I’ll meet you right here at dark,” Jack answered.

I knew he’d say something like that. Jack likes to hunt as much as I do.

It has been revealed that we all saw many deer that day, but all the bucks were small. None of us fired a shot.

But I came very close to filling my tag on the second day of the hunt. It drizzled again, and I just ambled along till 10 o’clock. Then I got real serious about my stillhunting. I don’t know why, but the really big bucks in that area seem to move mostly from 10 in the morning till about 1 in the afternoon.

About noon I spotted a deer in thick oak brush 200 yards ahead. We were both on a plateau. The animal was a significant one, so I assumed he was a buck, and I started moving in on him. My stalking was quiet because everything was wet, but I couldn’t close the distance very fast in that thick brush, and the deer kept moving away from me as he browsed.

According to recent reports, at one point I saw part of his rack, just enough to know the antlers were in the trophy class. The excitement ended when I tried to cut him off at the edge of the plateau. When I got there, he was gone. I’ll never know whether that buck sensed my presence or went off on a predetermined course.

Sources indicate that when Jack and I got back to camp two bucks were on the game pole. Robbie had nailed a five-pointer with his 7-mm. Remington Magnum rifle equipped with a Leupold scope. Bruce’s deer was also a five-pointer, but the antlers were heavier. Bruce collected his venison with a Winchester Model 70 .30/06 rigged with a Leupold scope.

When we awoke the third morning, the dad-gummed drizzle was still with us. I suited up in my Browning raingear and filled my pockets with dried fruits and jerky. I knew it would be another long day before I could bake myself beside the wood stove in the cooktent. I dropped Jack off on the trail and then drove on and parked near the area I had hunted the day before.

Industry observers note that A slight breeze was coming down off the mountain, so I decided to stillhunt into it and get farther back into rougher country. About 9 o’clock I started into a 400-yard-wide canyon and began working up toward one rim. I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

Then I looked at them through my Bausch & Lomb 7 x 35 binoculars. Both were definitely in the trophy class. It was fairly late in our hunt, so I decided it was best to cash in on one of them. I’d make the stalk and decide which rack was best when I got within range.

I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

It has been revealed that I eased on through the oak brush for about 200 yards and busted out a doe. She pushed on ahead of me. I didn’t think she would spook the bucks, but I watched them for several minutes to make sure. They continued feeding away from me up the slope. I could keep them in sight at this point because they were still in a clearing.

I eased back into some cover and stalked ahead for about 45 minutes while the drizzle came on stronger and stronger. During that time I didn’t see the bucks, because they had moved into a patch of brush, but I was pretty sure they were still nearby. I would have seen them if they had moved out on that slope. There was a 75-yard-wide opening at the top of the canyon, and I would have seen or heard them if they had run back toward me or along the canyon bottom.

An additional 30 minutes passed before I decided I couldn’t be more than 200 yards from the deer, but I still couldn’t see them — the patch of brush was up to 10 feet tall. Then I busted out a doe again. She crashed along toward the bucks. I figured they’d spook, so I took off at a dead run for an opening 20 yards ahead of me. If I was going to do any good, I had to shoot in a hurry.

Just as I broke into the opening, three deer ran into view. Two were the bucks I’d been stalking; the third was still bigger. He was lagging behind, and even in the split-second I had to shoot, I knew he had the best rack by far.

Sources indicate that my handloaded Nosler 125-grain bullet flew 300 yards, ripped into the buck’s heart-lung area, and blew up. He stumbled, hit the ground, and lay still.

When I examined the antlers — six unbelievably massive tines on the right side and five on the left — I knew I had killed the finest trophy buck I’d ever seen, but I had no idea that he was the best typical mule deer ever taken. The enormous body of the deer concerned me most at the moment.

Industry observers note that normally we can drive a vehicle close to our kills and then drag the deer out to the 4WD. But I was way back in rough country, and we couldn’t approach with a vehicle. It would have been impossible for me to drag that deer very far by myself.

Recent findings suggest that I decided to hike out to the Jeep and drive back to camp for help. Since Robbie and Bruce had already killed their bucks, the odds were they would be in camp. They were. We went back to my deer, dressed and quartered it, and packed the quarters and the head out to the vehicle. When we returned to camp we found Jack waiting for us. He needed some help with a heavy-antlered five-pointer he’d killed with his .270 Weatherby Magnum. By the time we got that buck out, the day and the hunt were finished.

Recent findings suggest that when I got home I took my buck’s head and cape to taxidermist Ed Schlier in San Antonio for mounting. He’s an official measurer for the Boone and Crockett Club, so we rough-scored the green antlers. Our preliminary figures indicated my buck would be among the top 10 listed in the typical-mule-deer category. That was exhilarating, but I didn’t think much more about it till one night several months later when my phone rang at 1 a.m.

According to recent reports, “Doug,” Ed blurted out, “I think your buck may be the best typical mule deer ever taken. I scored the antlers this evening, and I couldn’t believe it when I came up with a total score of two-hundred twenty-six! That’s nine better than the previous world-record typical mule deer. I’ve been double-checking my figures for hours, but they always come out the same. If they hold up with Boone and Crockett officials, you’ve got a upcoming world record. I figured that news was worth waking you up.”.

It sure was, but it was just the beginning.

The North American Major Game Award Program — jointly sponsored by the Boone and Crockett Club and the National Rifle Association — requires that any big-game trophy likely to win an award must be rescored by a panel of judges. Accordingly, I sent the mounted head off to the program headquarters in Washington, DC.

Recent findings suggest that in February 1974 the program coordinator phoned me and invited me to attend the Fifteenth North American Big Game Awards meeting on March 24 in Atlanta, Georgia. I guessed my buck had proven good enough to win some kind of award, but I was too busy to go to Atlanta.

That was my position till I received several more calls from other program officials. They told me that if I missed the awards meeting, I would very much regret it later, so I scraped together some cash, cancelled several appointments, and flew to Atlanta.

Recent findings suggest that at the banquet I was presented with the award for the best typical mule deer taken during the most recent three-year award period. I also received official recognition for taking a upcoming world record. In addition I won the Sagamore Hill Award, which is given only to hunters whose outstanding trophies are of great distinction. This award is the highest given by the Boone and Crockett Club. Only one may be given during any big-game-award period, and only 10 have been presented during the club’s history.

I was stunned. When I think about it, even today, I’m still stunned.

Former shooting editor Jim Carmichel wrote a short sidebar about his predictions for the next record-book mule deer.

Industry observers note that bagging a trophy mule deer hinges on four key factors: 1) luck, 2) hunting skill, 3) a firm determination to pass up lesser deer, 4) a carefully conducted survey of the areas likely to produce significant mule-deer bucks at a predetermined point in time. The last three are more or less under the control of the hunter, but the fourth requires a basic understanding of trophy development.

In a recent development, A look at the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book highlights that a large percentage of trophy mule deer have consistently been taken from certain fairly well-defined regions. Equally significant is that the trophy heads from these regions have been taken within specific time periods. During the early 1960’s, for example, a good number of high-ranking bucks were taken at the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in New Mexico. It’s no secret that certain areas tend to provide the natural requirements (such as a rich mineral diet) necessary for the development of significant antlers, and that certain genetic strains of deer tend to produce big racks. Arizona’s Kaibab area, to give but one example, is one of the regions well known for its ability to grow large-antlered mule deer. However, this doesn’t mean that these areas always abound with record-busting bucks. This is where the vital time element enters the picture.

Read Next: The Story of the Allison Buck, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History.

It has been revealed that if a big-buck-producing area is allowed to rest for a few seasons, with little or no hunting pressure, the bucks grow old and develop larger and larger antlers. Then word gets around about all the big bucks to be found there, and hunting pressure increases. In three or four years all the big trophy bucks have been killed off. When trophies become hard to find, the hunting pressure drops off, and the cycle begins again.

The smart trophy hunter keeps track of the best areas and keeps a discerning eye on the hunting pressure in these places. The idea, of course, is to get there a season or two ahead of the crowd.

#21755. Oregon (Yes, Oregon) Is the Best Hunting and Fishing State in America

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2440 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Oregon (Yes, Oregon) Is the Best Hunting and Fishing State in America

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, legs shortened on the tripod shooting sticks, rifle secure in the saddle, I eased the setup onto a small rise in front of me.
  • According to recent reports, A quick range reading followed by another confirmed the distance, 236 yards.
  • When I twisted the scope’s throw lever to 18X, the whitetail filled the field of view.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, legs shortened on the tripod shooting sticks, rifle secure in the saddle, I eased the setup onto a small rise in front of me. As I crawled into position, a buck materialized in the scope. It had no idea I was there.

According to recent reports, A quick range reading followed by another confirmed the distance, 236 yards. The evening air was dead calm.

When I twisted the scope’s throw lever to 18X, the whitetail filled the field of view. The shot was simple: one bullet from a Browning 6.8 Western dropped the deer, and my 2026 season was off to a good start.

Sources indicate that from the oak-studded knob on which I shot, I could see the North Umpqua River meandering through the valley below. It was on this river that I caught my first summer steelhead, at age 4, in 1968. In 1986 I shot my first wild turkey from the same area. That hunt sparked a 40-year passion chasing these grand birds.

As I walked up on the high-racked buck, the river’s unique beauty was captivating. I wasn’t looking at just any whitetail, but a prized Columbia whitetail. Here we have the only huntable population of these special deer in the world. I was exactly one hour and 20 minutes from my home in Western Oregon.

Sources indicate that almost 50 years to the day prior, I shot my very first deer — a Columbia blacktail. That buck came less than 15 miles from my home. Over the decades I’ve shot some dandy blacktails and seen bigger ones that outsmarted me. I rank consistently killing a mature trophy Columbia blacktail as the most challenging of all massive game hunting in North America. The habitat they call home is vast, varied and as dense as a tropical rainforest in places.

Less than a week after punching the whitetail tag I was in Oregon’s Coast Range. I saw seven bears in four days before shooting a mature, sleek-coated beauty. My wife and I love bear meat; she even renders the fat for cooking. It’s great this time of year.

Industry observers note that in the spring I hunted bears in the same area of the Coast Range. I passed 27 bears in seven days before pulling the trigger on a nice bruin.

Earlier this month, friends and I got serious about duck hunting public land on nearby rivers, as we always do this time of year. The first two hunts found us targeting wood ducks. I shot seven-bird limits of the gorgeous little ducks each time out. The following trip was a mix of mallards and woodies, and after that, an all-mallard limit. Excellent eating, all of them.

Recent findings suggest that one morning was extra special, as I achieved something I’d been trying to pull off for three seasons. The morning was foggy and wood ducks aggressively poured into the small spread of decoys. Shots were close. I took seven wood ducks along with a pair of honkers. While driving home with the double limit I got a text from a nearby landowner. A big flock of turkeys was back on his property. He asked if I’d come shoot some, as they were becoming a nuisance.

In recent years Oregon created a special hunt for problematic fall and winter turkeys. It’s called a beardless turkey permit and with it you can shoot three turkeys without visible beards, on each of the three available permits that are purchased over the counter. It’s a depredation hunt that was put in place to deter large flocks of fall turkeys from congregating on private property, causing damage and leaving messy gifts that are a health concern to pets and livestock. Since funding to trap and relocate turkeys was cut in the state, turkey numbers have exploded in many counties. It’s common to see multiple flocks a day of 100 or more turkeys, all fall and winter long, in several places around Oregon.

I hurried home, grabbed Echo, my pudelpointer, and headed out for the turkeys. Echo is almost 13 years old. She’s hunted fall turkeys every year of her life. Oregon is one of a handful of Western states that allows the use of dogs for fall turkey hunting. It’s one of my favorite hunts of the year and Echo loves it. For Kona, my 10-year-old male pudelpointer who I lost to an intestinal torsion this past September, this was his favorite hunt of all. It was hard heading afield without him, for the first time.

But Echo didn’t skip a beat. After some searching we finally located the flock of turkeys. There were 46 of them, all hens, jakes, and jennies. They fed on the edge of a grassy meadow, heading uphill toward a patch of Douglas fir timber. When the time was right, I sent Echo. She ran at the flock as fast as her aging legs could carry her. She’d done this many times in her life. She knew the drill. If all the birds flushed, I’d call her back, we’d sneak into the timber, set up and call the flock back in. That didn’t happen.

This time Echo caught the turkeys by surprise. A few flew into the trees but most burrowed into thick blackberries and tall, green ferns. Echo struck the perfect point and held it until I arrived. Turkeys often hold tight as quail. When I got to Echo, a jake made a run for it. It didn’t make it far. At the shot, the rest of the flock scurried, some running, some taking wing. I shot another bird on the run, then dropped one more from the air. Echo couldn’t gather them fast enough. Finally, my bird trifecta was completed.

According to recent reports, we ate birds for dinner that night, and Tiffany whipped up multiple dishes for a big church potluck the following day. Everyone enjoyed the local bounty, and there was an extra sense of pride among the elderly men who used to hunt.

It has been revealed that I’ve been fortunate to hunt much of the country, and even lived in Alaska for a stint in the 1990s. When it comes to hunting and fishing, I’ve found no other state that matches what Oregon has to offer. It boasts hunting opportunities for 12 big game species, including four subspecies of deer. It has the best turkey hunting I’ve seen, with 14 tags available a year, including three spring toms. Thirty-three of the 41 recognized waterfowl species can be hunted here, along with bonus Eurasian wigeon which are becoming more frequent. Wigeon are my favorite duck to hunt and they thrive in the valleys and coast.

If you’re into predator hunting, coyotes and bobcats abound statewide. Mountain lions are now classified as substantial game in Oregon. In the past few years I’ve called in eight cougars, shooting the last one at 12 paces, using a shotgun. Last year I caught 11 different lions on trail cameras in one morning, all within 25 miles of my home–seven were within two miles. Cougars are thick, I wish we could hunt them with hounds as numbers are out of control. But some of our game laws make zero sense.

Recent findings suggest that most recently Oregon made national news for the infamous Oregon Initiative Petition 28. IP 28 didn’t even appear on the November ’26 ballot. Yet, just about every blurb on the topic for the past year made it appear certain Oregon was going to lose all hunting and fishing privileges. Much of the press and pursuers of clickbait chastised Oregonians, ignorant of the full story and who the players were. In the fine print, IP 28 was absurd not only to hunters and anglers, but cattle ranchers, farmers, pet owners and more folks in our state.

I was stunned at the number of fellow outdoorsmen who threw Oregon sportsmen under the bus, telling them to move from the state. Oregon is not the problem. Our issue is that the state is largely governed by people in three cities. The hunting and fishing population outside those city limits is large, and the many animals thriving in the game-rich state know no such boundaries nor are they aware of the people who set the rules. One hunting or fishing trip to our great state will reveal how special it truly is.

According to recent reports, for the past 26 years I’ve made a living as a full-time writer and wildlife photographer. For 14 of those years I hosted hunting and fishing TV shows. I’ve written more than 4,200 magazine articles and 17 books with more in the works. I couldn’t have done it if not for living in Western Oregon, in the little town of Walterville — named after people on my wife’s side of the family.

Minutes from my home there’s something to hunt or fish for every day of the year. I live on the McKenzie River, a tributary of the famed Willamette River. I caught my first spring chinook salmon from the McKenzie in the 1960s. Over the decades, it, along with the Willamette River, have produced thousands of springers and loads of summer steelhead and rainbow trout for my family. Growing up fishing these rivers  spoiled me.

Recent findings suggest that the Willamette River is massive, wide, and challenging to fish in places. Downstream from where the Willamette flows into the mighty Columbia River, you’ll find some of the world’s best salmon and sturgeon fishing.

Sources indicate that the McKenzie River is a blue ribbon rated trout stream, one of the best in the country. Growing up, word traveled fast when movie stars were on the water, most presenting dry flies to try and entice stunning redsides.

Sources indicate that A few miles from my home, Theodore Roosevelt loved to fish for rainbow trout. I know where he stayed and the holes he liked to fish. Rumor has it–from some of my wife’s relatives who homesteaded the McKenzie River Valley in the mid-1800s–it was among Roosevelt’s favorite rivers to fish, both for the trout and the sheer beauty the region offered. Roosevelt would be happy to know that the place he so loved is now teeming with wildlife, including elk that carry his name.

In fourth grade I began trapping. My parents took turns taking me to check traps before school. For sets close to home, I’d ride my bike. Beaver, raccoon, coyote, red fox and bobcat were some of the target species. I skinned the catch after school. This continued into my freshman year of high school, until sports consumed my life. Trapping greatly educated me about the land and the animals that live there. It also allowed me to make some money so I could fish in the summer months, rather than work.

It has been revealed that in the 1970s, most duck hunting I experienced was on the rivers. In my formative years Dad, Grandpa and I spent many days together in duck and goose blinds.

Sources indicate that less than an hour from my home the first ring-necked pheasants were introduced to the continental United States. Birds arrived by sea in 1882, from China. Dad and grandpa shared many stories of incredible pheasant hunts they had in the 1950s and ‘60s. “Best pheasant hunting in the country,” Grandpa mentioned. He wasn’t wrong. Today, we don’t pester what few pheasants remain in the valley. But parts of Eastern Oregon are flourishing with ring-necks. A few years back, Echo and I secured a limit of ducks, pheasants and valley quail on one of our best days, ever.

Valley quail and mountain quail thrive around my home. Getting on multiple coveys a day is common. The occasional ruffed grouse is put up in the valley, but they’re more prevalent in the foothills of the Cascades and Coast Range. Just above ruffed grouse in the mountains are blue grouse. When I was a kid we never saw a blue grouse below 2,000 feet. Today we shoot a lot of the big birds at and below 500 feet. More than once I’ve taken valley and mountain quail, blue and ruffed grouse on the same day. Truly special hunts, all of them.

Recent findings suggest that in mid-September band-tailed pigeons are the target. They occupy both mountain ranges and parts of the valley floor. In my days of youth the daily limit was seven, today it’s only two. Still, dogs love these hunts, as does my 86-year-old father. Intercepting speeding birds as they fly ridgelines in search of berries, minerals and water makes for challenging shooting and steep country retrieves.

In the fall we chase Western gray squirrels. Kona loved treeing gray squirrels almost as much as he reveled in fall turkey hunting. The furry tree-dwellers are delicious.

In a recent development, for decades, cackling Canada geese have flocked to the Willamette Valley to graze on rye grass. The Willamette Valley is dubbed The Grass Seed Capital Of The World, and this prime food attracts loads of big game and waterfowl. Minimas — the smallest of the cackling Canada geese — regularly funnel into big decoy spreads in flocks of 10,000 or more. Words can’t be heard over the screaming little geese.

It has been revealed that thirty minutes from home, in multiple directions, is the best duck hunting I’ve found anywhere in the country. One day you’re hunting wigeon and pintails in flooded fields; the next, picking greenheads in tiny creeks surrounded by tall trees. You can regularly shoot a seven drake limit of wood ducks on public waters and private land filbert orchards, what outsiders call hazelnuts. The valleys hold some of the world’s best soil for filbert farming. As these orchards have expanded in recent years, wood duck and mallard numbers continue to grow because they love feasting on the nuts. Today there are more wood ducks than I ever recall seeing in my 51 years of hunting them.

As I finalize these words, I’m preparing for the next several days afield, all near home. Tomorrow I’ll be hunting wood ducks on the river. The day after that, checking my 75 trail cameras set in the nearby hills. And the day after that I head to the Coast Range to hunt secretive Roosevelt elk in the rainforest. Last November I took a 340-class Roosevelt 35 minutes from home, my biggest Roosy bull to date.

Recent findings suggest that there’s no better place to be, doing what I love the most. Oregon is a grand place to grow up, and to grow old.

Industry News: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Finally Resigns as Plea Deal in Elk Poaching Scandal Draws Hunter Outrage

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker.
  • In a recent development, “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov.
  • In a recent development, harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker. Harshbarger took a plea deal on Nov. 9 to dismiss five of seven charges related to illegally killing two bull elk in the region he represents.

In a recent development, “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov. Brad Little’s chief of staff, Zach Hauge, in response to Harshbarger’s resignation, obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Maintaining the integrity, credibility and effective operation of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission remains a top priority for Gov. Little.”.

In a recent development, harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives. The former commissioner stepped away from commission duties once he was charged, but retained his seat until this week while the case continued, effectively leaving the position vacant.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Says He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

It has been revealed that “I understand everyone deserves their day in court, but commissioners are charged with making and upholding our regulations,” Nick Fasciano, executive director of the Idaho Wildlife Federation, tells Outdoor Life. “And we do expect them to be held to a higher standard. The whole thing is disappointing.”.

The commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists. Each member of the commission can serve two four-year terms, and no more than four commissioners can come from the same political party. Harshbarger is a farmer in Ashton, Idaho. It’s an area known for massive chunks of public land and substantial grain and potato operations.

According to recent reports, “I love our wildlife and the community we live in,” Harshbarger’s profile read on the commission’s website before it was removed. “We have a lot of challenges, and I am excited to help continue to solve them. What an amazing place to live and work.”.

In a recent development, harshbarger pled guilty to hunting without a tag and shooting across a road. The remaining five charges, which are being dismissed in exchange for his guilty plea, are two illegal big-game kills, hunting from a vehicle, failure to retrieve game, and trespass (one bull was on private property).

When news of Harshbarger’s plea deal went public, hunters and anglers started contacting regional IDFG offices and the governor’s office to demand his removal. The plea deal means his penalties could be as low as $500 and a one-year hunting suspension when he’s sentenced Dec. 9.

Frustration has also boiled over on social media around Harshbarger’s case.

In a recent development, “Wake up Governor Little and do the right thing,” one Instagram user commented on the news of the plea deal, prior to Harshbarger’s resignation. “You and Senator Risch are already working to sell off our public lands and now you won’t step in to protect our wild game. Shame on you two.”.

Harshbarger was appointed by Gov. Little in 2024.

“Public trust is difficult to earn and easily lost,” wrote Idaho state Rep. David Leavitt in an email sent to Little on Tuesday that called for Harshbarger’s dismissal. “Maintaining that trust requires us to uphold the same principles regardless of who is involved. Idaho citizens deserve nothing less.”.

Recent findings suggest that little is also now in charge of appointing the director of IDFG. The commission did that until this year, when Little signed a publicly opposed bill into law changing the procedure from a seven-person decision to a one-person appointment by the governor, with confirmation by the state Senate.

Recent findings suggest that “Commissioners and the director now serve at the pleasure of the governor,” Fasciano says. “The commission is not empowered to boot out one of their own members even if they were so inclined.”.

Current IDFG director Jim Fredericks, a career fisheries biologist, was already leading the agency when the new law took effect July 1, making him the state’s last director selected by the commission.

Read Next: Montana Man Banned from Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull.

“The actual department of Fish and Game is going to take some heat for this [Harshbarger incident], but they weren’t the decision makers here,” Fasciano states. “The commission and the director were not able to drive a resolution here and they are also not responsible for the sentencing. A lot of frustration is going to be directed toward them, that isn’t their fault.”.

Warm feet allow proper blood flow, moving heat to other parts of your body. When you get cold, it can make for a miserable outdoor experience—which is where heated socks come into play.

While there are plenty of warm socks out there, heated socks take cozy to the next level, with rechargeable batteries powering them up. To find the warmest pairs, we tested the best heated socks for both men and women through hours of hunting, camping, and just spending time outside.

Designed for comfort and performance with a moisture-wicking wool blend, these socks are ready for the elements.

Fortunately, Gerbing used a microwire in its design for maximum comfort—no wire digging into your skin.

Sources indicate that these are the most expensive heated socks we reviewed; however, the quality and performance are well worth the price. Plus, the heating elements are backed by Gerbing’s lifetime warranty, so you have peace of mind.

You can charge them simultaneously, and in just a few hours, they’re fully loaded and ready to go. However, they can also be a negative. Because of their size, they sometimes struggle to stay in place and can bunch up in the socks. Savior is also a good choice for the budget-conscious shopper—you can get a pair for under $80. Industry observers note that if you’re looking for the best heated socks for hunting, look no further than this pair from Snow Deer. ActionHeat is well-known for making outstanding heated gear, and these rechargeable heated socks are no exception. They feature an ultra-fine carbon fiber heating panel that offers four levels of heat, ranging up to 140 degrees. They’re plenty warm for even the coldest of days.

The socks come with a remote control that allows you to easily adjust the heat settings while wearing them. Powered by an ActionHeat 3.74V battery along with FAR infrared heating and heat-reflective technology, they provide warmth for more than seven hours of use on a single charge. They’re made of a comfortable and stretchy cotton and spandex blend that holds up well with frequent wear. When it comes to quality, ActionHeat doesn’t skimp out.

In a recent development, the Ororo Mojave heated socks were designed based on valuable feedback from customers, so they have a bunch of features we appreciate. The upcoming sock design is made with a combination of cotton, CoolMax, polyester, and spandex through a unique terry loop knitting method, which gives them a more padded and cushioned feel. Just as vital, they are moisture-wicking and breathable, pulling sweat away from the skin to keep your feet dry. The breathability factor makes these socks ideal for outdoor activities like hiking or winter sports like skiing or snowshoeing.

The heating element is located at the bottom part of the foot, providing 70 percent more coverage than Ororo’s previous model. It’s powered by 2000mAh batteries that provide up to 11 hours of use. One note: These socks are made of 60 percent cotton, so they are prone to shrinking in the wash.

FieldSheer heated socks come in both men’s and women’s sizes and designs. They have a compression-like feel with ample arch support to prevent foot pain. They also sport a seamless construction, so there’s no irritation or itching. Thanks to the no-slip band, these socks never fell down while I was wearing them. In terms of comfort, I also really liked the contoured battery, which allowed the battery to fit snugly against my calf.

These Fieldsheer socks are controlled via a mobile app. There, I was able to adjust the heat setting and monitor the battery life. What’s really nice is that you can control each sock separately. Plus, you can even connect other heated gear—like heated vests or heated gloves—to the same profile. I personally really appreciated the battery life percentage monitoring capability. Even though the battery is the smallest out of all the ones we reviewed, it still lasts up to 10 hours on the lowest heat setting.

In a recent development, with the high percentage of merino wool, these socks have a solid heat retention rating. However, they offer less coverage than others on our list—the heated area only covers from the upper part of your sole up to your toes.

Through years of wearing heated socks, I have narrowed down exactly what makes a quality pair. The style and comfort may fluctuate depending on the brand, but the factors below should apply to all. Of course, you’ll also want to take into consideration your own needs to make sure they’re met.

After handpicking which heated socks to include in our review process, here’s how I evaluated each pair during testing and research:.

When dealing with anything that depends on battery power, the type of battery is important. You don’t want to invest in a pricey heated sock just for the battery to die. Rechargeable batteries are cost-effective and convenient. They are also more environmentally friendly, reducing the excess of disposable batteries in landfills.

Recent findings suggest that however, rechargeable batteries have limited charging cycles and will require replacement. Batteries such as lithium-ion may provide more stable and reliable performance and minimize charging times.

Socks normally come in grouped sizing; they are “one size fits most.” Since most heated socks for men and women come up over the calf, factor your calf size into your size choice. Most of these socks are unisex, so if you have a need women’s size or a wide option, take that into consideration as you weigh your pros and cons. Always refer to the socks’ size chart to determine the best fit for your feet.

Recent findings suggest that durability is always high on my consideration list. When making a gear investment, you want something that is going to last but also that won’t break the bank. Consider the materials used. Wool, for instance, has a high heat retention rating and will last through seasons of use.

Also think about frequency of wear. What is your intended use? An avid outdoor enthusiast who aims to wear their heated socks almost daily will require a more durable option than someone who will just wear them a handful of times for weekend adventures.

Industry observers note that yes, heated socks are a great investment. I’ve worn them for years and they’re a game-changer. Of course, it also depends on your specific needs and intended use.

Recent findings suggest that the lifespan of your heated socks will vary depending on use and base materials. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for washing and drying and avoid using harsh detergents to help them last longer. As for battery life, rechargeable batteries will slow down over time and start losing their charging power. Fortunately, if the sock itself is still holding up well, you can just purchase a latest replacement battery to remedy that problem.

Industry observers note that yes, each pair of electrical socks comes with a mesh laundry bag. Remove the batteries, cover the plug (if applicable), and clip to secure the pocket. Wash on delicate and hang to dry. That said, be sure to check the care instructions for your specific socks before washing.

Heated socks are a prime example of how advanced technology for outdoor gear has become. When choosing the best heated socks for you, weigh the performance of the batteries and the durability of the material with how comfortable the socks are. You want to get the most out of your footwear, so we recommend investing in a pair that will keep you doing the outdoor activities you love for longer, like the Gerbing Ultimate or the Snow Deer heated socks. Your feet will be happy, and so will you.

Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. #21749. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2460 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The substantial whitetail buck and I badly startled each other.
  • Recent findings suggest that after the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding.
  • But then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The substantial whitetail buck and I badly startled each other. In the steady rain patter, he apparently didn’t hear me until I’d stillhunted very close to his cedar clump shelter. I almost came unglued when he exploded into view, too spooked to even snort.

Recent findings suggest that after the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding. So much for my semi-frantic snapshot.

But then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence. Without snow, it took awhile to slowly, alertly follow up. I found the heart-shot buck. That terminal crash noise came from his failing to clear a windfall when the carburetor quit for keeps.

Recent findings suggest that that’s stillhunting at its best. Unlike the prolonged tedium of trail watching or waiting out a drive, stillhunting’s uptight anticipation is an ongoing thrill. When the action does come, it’s often sudden, without warning. Don’t hunt this way if you have a weak heart.

Very old-timers like my 87-year-old father tell me that forest stillhunting was far more common decades ago. Maybe today’s urban hunters don’t trust their stealth and woodcraft skills. Although not an easy way to take woodland game, including elk, the bottom-line reality is that stillhunting can produce game when other tactics cannot.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, a lone-wolf hunter can’t make drives to himself. Even when sufficient manpower is available, effective drives require thorough knowledge of both the terrain and how local deer use it. If game chooses not to move because it fed well last night, lacks sexual ambition just now or doesn’t like the prevailing weather, trail watching is usually hopeless. For that matter, many mule deer and most elk and moose simply don’t stick that much to established trails.

It has been revealed that the stillhunter is free of such vagaries. Instead of hoping game will come to him, he goes to it — although stillhunting is not the stalking of game already located. Tactically, he has two top priorities. First, to move quietly and alertly, his course basically dictated by wind, terrain and possibly sun direction. Second, to discover game before it sees, hears or smells him. The stillhunter must play a lone-hand game — two hunters seem to make not twice, but four times the noise of one hunter.

Industry observers note that slow movement is a must. A stillhunter covering ground too promptly simply can’t look well enough for concealed game. He also can’t help making extra noise to be picked up by critters who depend on acute hearing every day of their lives to stay out of trouble. They easily detect high frequency noises (including any rustles, squeaks or metallic clinks from our gear and garb) that we often can’t hear.

Recent findings suggest that the real trick in stillhunting is to do the looking and the moving as two separate functions. If you forget everything else, remember that! When you attempt to look for game and move your feet at the same time, sooner or later you will make unwanted noise — snapping a brittle twig, tripping noisily or whatever.

Recent findings suggest that don’t follow any set rhythm of taking a set number of steps, then stopping. Instead, consider the area that you can see from where you stand as one vision zone. I never move until this zone, of up to 180° ahead and to both sides, has been totally studied.

Industry observers note that A vision zone may range out only 50 feet in dense woods or 200-plus yards in more open country. Depending on the extent of the zone, terrain and cover, it may take 30 seconds or several minutes of methodical looking. Often a promising area is worth the time to just sit for extra eyeballing.

Recent findings suggest that don’t expect to see a full-blown deer or elk looming up ahead like calendar artwork. Look for just parts of the animal as clues. Most forest visuals are vertical lines — tree trunks, etc. An out-of-place horizontal line may be a log or the outline of a deer’s back. A smudge of dull yellow may be autumn leaves or an elk rump. Wide-field binoculars help greatly on such details.

Recent findings suggest that once, while hunting in the Cascade Mountains, my eye caught a tiny movement ahead. A broad leaf twitching with the breeze? But there was no breeze and, in that evergreen thicket, no deciduous leaves. I waited some minutes, then spotted the movement again for what it was — a blacktail doe’s ear twitching as its owner listened. When she finally moved, right behind her came a shootable buck.

After searching a visual zone (and listening, too), select a route for the next few feet or yards, based on avoidance of brush contact or other potential noise. Footwork is important. Short steps are quietest. They offer best control of shifting your balance if you ease your foot down and feel a twig likely to snap under full weight. Also, only with short steps can you come down slowly and silently on your toes or the ball of your foot. Long steps force the heel down first, making it much more likely that you will snap twigs or make a soft but tell-tale thud.

Sources indicate that want some expert stillhunting lessons? Simply watch a house cat on the prowl for birds or field mice. Slow movement, long look-listen pauses, obvious patience and great concentration are what make felines the finest stillhunters in nature. Once, in Washington’s mountains, I watched a mountain lion on the prowl. This best-of-all deer hunter resembles a magnified house cat at work.

Major or small, hunting cats are superb at using concealment. You should do likewise. Very often, unseen game ahead will hear you. By moving slowly with minimum noise, you may sound much like just another deer. But the listening quarry will be watching in your direction for visual confirmation. Don’t slow yourself any more than necessary. I use camouflage makeup to make my pale face less visible against dark forest backdrop.

If you can move quietly in some kind of concealment, use that route rather than an easier-looking, more open course. Stick to shadows; avoid sunlit patches. When possible, hunt with the sun behind you. Go over ridgetops with caution, using brush or timber cover. If the hilltop lacks cover, try crawling. Of course, stillhunting must be done into the wind or at least across it — never downwind. Although human sense of smell is pretty pathetic, sometimes the barnyard odor of elk ahead can be detected.

Sources indicate that often a stillhunter has the option of following fresh game tracks. Except under ideal conditions, such as newly introduced snow, one-man tracking demands so much attention that the stillhunter is distracted while he should be looking for actual game. More than once, deer or elk have surprised me, costing me a shot simply because I was distracted by some interesting tracks. If you start trailing, remember that the maker of these tracks may be bedded down somewhere ahead and almost certainly watching his backtrail. To get anywhere close to it will require extremely good stillhunting.

In a recent development, the lay of the land can be friend or foe. Ridges and hills offer chances to surprise game on the other side. Flat country is tougher because it offers few elevation advantages to the hunter. Although knowing the area always helps, it’s not truly essential for stillhunting. Once, a young stillhunter in our party, new to the place, nailed a whitetail buck the second morning. A fast learner, he capped that next year by pussyfooting close enough to a Cascades bull elk to take him with a bow.

The inexperienced stillhunter is often tempted to work mature evergreen timber, where dense shade means little underbrush. But closely spaced conifers self-prune their branches profusely, forming a noisy layer of dead twigs. Such forests can be hunted only when there’s enough wind noise to cover the hunter’s snap-crackle-pop progress. Unless soggy from rain or wet snow, dead leaves are another audio booby trap.

According to recent reports, some timber is open enough to have a good growth of clover or grass, particularly attractive to elk. By contrast, dense coniferous forests contain little ground-level browse to attract feeding game, but they often provide good escape cover when hunting pressure is on. In unseasonably warm weather, the cool shade of thick evergreen timber invites game. In cold weather, the evergreen canopy traps radiant ground heat for considerably warmer bedding than more open forests.

In a recent development, where evergreen timber is lacking, game makes the best of thick brushy cover or tall grasses — the latter is commonly a deer favorite. In real cold or after rain, any warming sun draws game to south or west-facing slopes.

Best time of day for stillhunting depends on several factors. Stillhunting as early as light permits may find game feeding or on the move to bedding. Ground litter then is less noisy, thanks to the night’s dampening dew. But if overnight frost has made fallen leaves ultra-brittle or has crusted the snow, better wait for some midday thawing.

Though rain or a moderate wind helps mask hunter movement sounds, strong winds are a mixed blessing. With their hearing impaired by too much wind, restless animals change location often rather than staying put. That aids the stillhunter, because moving game is far easier to see. But wind-jittery animals, up on their feet and watching for danger they can’t hear, can spot the hunter more readily. Fortunately, a stiff wind covers his extra noise if the stillhunter sticks to thicker cover for extra concealment.

Worst of all are those dead-calm Indian summer days, when even your shadow seems to make a racket in the dried-out forest. The only option, then, is to hunt terrain where game can be spotted at a considerable distance (example: from one ridge to another).

Recent findings suggest that some cover simply can’t be stillhunted. Swampy terrain is impossibly noisy, all the more if there’s any ice to be broken. Dry, fluffy snow can be fairly quiet for walking. But typical autumn snow, heavy and wet, is composed of oversize, many-pointed flakes. Each step compression-shatters untold thousands of such crystalline flakes. That accounts for the appallingly loud squeakiness. Until it’s settled, breaking its flakes in the process, such snow is no good for stillhunting. The settling process may take two or three days unless a thaw speeds it.

Industry observers note that snow characteristics may vary with terrain. North-facing snow is little affected by the weak sun of late autumn, but snow on southern and western slopes settles promptly with a few hours of sun.

Sources indicate that the stillhunter must remember that weather affects game’s likely location. The first serious snowfall often causes deer to hole up in the shelter of thick, low-branching evergreens, where they may stay 48 to 72 hours, believe it or not, even during the rut. Hungry when they finally leave cover, deer then are likely to feed during the day. But until they start moving, the pristine snow will be barren of tracks, leading to the false conclusion that all game has moved out.

Industry observers note that of course, game does move out of high country when massive snowstorms hit. Hunting deer and elk on such vertical migration routes is often considered a trail-watching game. The stillhunter can cover more territory to learn where game is moving — and if it’s moving.

Gear and clothing are critical in stillhunting. Soft leather boots with crepe soles are almost moccasin-quiet but treacherous in steep, wet or rocky terrain. Classic, Maine-style, rubber shoepacs make quiet steps. Their rounded sole edges are not as likely to shear-snap noisy twigs as stiffer, sharp-edged soles do. With any other rubber footwear, wear enough socks to prevent empty space around the foot from audibly pumping air at each step.

Recent findings suggest that harder, composition soles with lugs are necessary to maintain life and limb in rough country. Alas, such footwear is noisier. The only consolation is that in country steep enough to require lug-soled boots, the stillhunter has a longer “working range” across canyons, etc., and is not quite as vulnerable to making noise as the close-range, flatland hunter. At times, I’ve carried soft sneakers in my daypack to slip on after climbing a ridge that demanded lug-soled, ankle-supportive boots. Another useful trick is to wear a pair of knit leg warmers running from knee-height to ankles. These muffle twig noise and grass swish.

Recent findings suggest that clothing choice is very simple. Whatever the material, it must be soft. Nylon, corduroy and stiff denim are too noisy. Wool and flannel are the great favorites for quiet movement. Some synthetics like orlon and acrylic are almost as good, depending on weave and nap. Rubberized raingear makes less noise than nylon or vinyl. Because a hat’s brim snags noisy branches, wear a cap. Again, wool or knitted acrylic is quietest. I made a simple, woolen pack cover to keep my backpack from imitating a snare drum when I hunker through overhanging branches.

For quiet carrying, a firearm’s barrel length is more critical than weight per se. Although carbines are best, one of my favorite woods rifles has a 24-inch barrel. I find a 26-inch barrel is just too easy to bang against branches. A timber riflescope should have at least a 30-foot field at 100 yards — more would be better, because forest shots are often at close-range game on the run. Yellow shooting glasses contrast brown deer and elk better against evergreen backgrounds.

According to recent reports, pocket hardware like keys, coins and cartridges must be handkerchief-wrapped to eliminate tell-tale clinking. When I rendezvoused with my deer-hunting daughter in the woods, her sardonic greeting was, “Hello, Santa!”.

It has been revealed that “Well before I saw you,” she continued, “I could hear you playing ‘Jingle Bells’. What’s in your pockets?”.

A ring of unwrapped keys, that’s what. And deer probably could hear it twice as well as she could.

Although usually not physically taxing, stillhunting is tiring if you do it right. What wears you out is the strain of constant vigilance. And I mean constant! About the time you relax or daydream, up bounds a buck or bull that makes good his escape because you weren’t mentally prepared to react quite fast enough. But if you’re a dedicated hunter, the high-tension hours of stillhunting are memorable whether you score or not.

This story, “Deer on the Prowl,” appeared in the January 1990 problem of Outdoor Life. Read more from this series:.

#21748. The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners.
  • To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other customers.
  • According to recent reports, those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other customers.

According to recent reports, those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:.

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Sources indicate that take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

According to recent reports, don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Sources indicate that don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

In a recent development, as trail runners, we move relatively swiftly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail people. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

Recent findings suggest that this is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail customers.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

Recent findings suggest that if you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy.

Sources indicate that don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more notable that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”.

In a recent development, so, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Sources indicate that technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other people and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

It has been revealed that don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

It has been revealed that if running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you blueprint to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

#21746. The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that marcus Caston, Mt.
  • According to recent reports, it’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe.
  • “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that marcus Caston, Mt. Bohemia, Mich. (Photo: Keri Bascetta).

According to recent reports, it’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe. Eyes shut tight, she shouts over the gathered skiers.

“Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head. “By your power, give us powder. Amen.” She is our shaman.

“Amen,” we all murmur along and mean it.

Recent findings suggest that the Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage. But on Michigan’s isolated Keweenaw Peninsula, known as “the fin,” Mount Bohemia has no shortage of true believers. And they’re not coming for the corduroy. This expert-only backcountry resort is ungroomed, technical, and seriously steep. Signs across the mountain are clear: NO BEGINNERS ALLOWED.

While skiers scour the globe for powder, Michigan has been sitting on one of the country’s most unlikely stashes. Bohemia sees almost 300 inches annually, with no snowmaking. Here, bad weather is usually good news. Arctic air sweeping over Lake Superior’s warmer water produces storms that bury the Keweenaw. This lake-effect snow is remarkably light and dry—the kind you’d travel to Utah or Japan to find.

On paper, Bohemia’s numbers seem modest: 900 vertical feet, 585 acres, and just two lifts. Yet over 90 percent of its runs are black diamond or better, including the region’s only triple-blacks. Boho has the untamed feel of backcountry skiing, minus the skinning. Its dozen or so named territories—mostly sprawling glade districts—each have distinct temperaments.

“It can take two or three visits before guests get a feel for the mountain,” says Vern Barber, Bohemia’s general manager.

Sources indicate that I spend one morning adrift in one of the territories, Extreme Backcountry, a half-mile-wide expanse of Bohemia’s toughest terrain. Its high-angle tree runs, cliff drops, and narrow chutes kept funneling me onto unexpected lines. Supposedly, somewhere out there is a frozen waterfall drop I never managed to find. I wasn’t going to hit it. I just wanted to look.

Now I’m farther out in Middle Earth, another territory, surfing Boho’s longest runs through twisting hardwoods. Less steep, but somehow more exhausting. This is where skiers come to explore, hunting for pockets of untouched powder.

I stop at a trail marked “Helm’s Deep.” It took several attempts to find this place. Even then, it felt like an accident. The entrance is just a gap interrupting the tangle of trees—my only way down. Two clicks of my poles, and I drop in.

Dry powder explodes on my first turn. Branches rake both sleeves as I weave between trunks. Each bank hides what lies ahead. I barrel over a blind rise straight toward a stand of maples. I slash hard right and spray snow against the bark. Off balance, I slip through a drift and down a steep-sided gully.

According to recent reports, “You’re rowdy,” I grunt as the trees finally open. With room to breathe, I find my rhythm. Ahead lie 30 yards of untracked pillows. I point my tips and charge.

Industry observers note that by the time I pop out at the bottom, a throng of skiers is already waiting. Not for a chairlift, but for a bus. Bohemia’s farthest backcountry runs spill onto Lac La Belle Road, where a fleet of buses collects those who make it out of the woods. Over four days, I’ve shuffled through far more bus lines than lift lines. With luck, the next shuttle will be the elusive ABBA bus, plastered with Swedish memorabilia and bumping “Dancing Queen.” Today, I’m not so lucky. I climb into a regular bus for the day’s last ride, legs shot.

As we pull into base, the parking lot is just getting started. Around a fire barrel, a haggard congregation passes bottles and joints. Skiers still in bibs boil noodles on camp stoves between RVs and Sprinter vans. This crowd feels familiar—as if every little ski hill I grew up on in Michigan sent its most adventurous regulars.

The village itself is a jumble of yurts, stitched together by gangways. It houses bars, a hostel, and a surprisingly elaborate Nordic spa. Its 30-person hot tub was dubbed “dude stew.” But Vern claims they don’t call it that anymore.

For a place that wears you out by noon, Boho has a strange amount of energy after dark. Inside the North Pole Bar, skiers running on beer and pasties belt out “Country Roads” with the band. The party stumbles outside to packed pools and saunas. Much later, some hooligans will hike halfway up the frontside and sled down on stolen cafeteria trays. I am one of them.

In a recent development, on my last morning at Mount Bohemia, a particularly nasty blizzard has blown in off Lake Superior. Word is spreading through the yurts: high winds and whiteout have shut down the lifts. The buses aren’t running.

Recent findings suggest that skiers gather at the back of the village, their helmets and jackets already covered in powder. Out of the blowing snow, a single snowcat materializes. Vern himself is behind the wheel. The wind forces him to park at an angle to wrestle the door open. Skiers cram aboard, a handful at a time, bound for the summit.

I join the others in line. We laugh and curse as the snowcat is swallowed again by the whiteout. Powder is piling up around our shins. Above us, the glades are already buried. I can’t feel my toes. It’s a perfect day.

Not a bad place for a pilgrimage.
