#21738. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1524 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • According to recent reports, despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

According to recent reports, despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

It has been revealed that on the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

Recent findings suggest that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden said, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

It has been revealed that linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

It has been revealed that survival promptly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling blueprint was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

In a recent development, unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden said. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

According to recent reports, when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden noted. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

Industry observers note that while Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden noted. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

It has been revealed that the development of heated gloves—like with heated vests—is one of the better innovations in outdoor wear. As much as we enjoy spending time in nature during the winter months, we hate cold hands. It’s hard to concentrate on your hunt or effectively work if your fingers are so cold you can no longer feel them. For anyone with arthritis or other hand pain, it can be downright painful to venture out in winter. Luckily, battery-operated heating elements are here to change the game.

According to recent reports, wading through the hundreds of different options to find the ideal gloves can be a chore. That’s why we’ve done the homework for you. It doesn’t matter if you need something for work or for ice fishing, we’ve got you covered with the best heated gloves available for cold weather.

When it comes to battery life, the Ororo heated gloves—which feature three heat settings—performed better than I expected. I was able to run the gloves on the maximum temperature setting for approximately three to four hours and on the medium setting for at least five. However, the low setting was where they really shined. These gloves ran for a solid eight hours on that setting. Because they were so warm even without turning on the electricity, I highly doubt I’ll ever use the medium and high settings.

My only real complaint is that I feel the dexterity could be better. The insulation makes the fingers a bit too fat for shooting a rifle or shotgun. But the grip on the palms and fingers has a tacky feel to it that’s perfectly suited for working with shovels or other hand tools where super fine control isn’t needed. I’ll be using these to clear the driveway of snow once winter returns to Michigan. These gloves would also be excellent for operating a tractor, ATV, or snowmobile in cold temperatures.

Sources indicate that the Savior gloves are plenty warm without an electric feature. But they also feature larger 2200 mAh batteries that help keep your fingers toasty through longer days outdoors. Because they are waterproof and thick, you can wear these gloves whenever there is snow or slush on the ground. The windproof quality makes them an excellent choice for work or riding a motorcycle, too. They are thick, so there is some dexterity loss. But Savior Heat made the button for heat control quite large, so you can easily operate it without removing the gloves.

Sources indicate that these gloves are a hair on the expensive side. But that’s to be expected for this battery size and durability. While we like these gloves best for work—like construction or ranch work—they are versatile enough to be used in a variety of outdoor scenarios.

Industry observers note that surprisingly, there are not a lot of dedicated hunting gloves featuring electronic heating. This pair is both windproof and waterproof—perfect for hunters who don’t like to head in once the weather takes a turn for the worst. The 7.4V battery packs will help the warming functions last through a full day in frigid temperatures, and the buttons are large enough that you can operate them while wearing the gloves. Plus, they have fingertips that can operate a touchscreen.

Industry observers note that the three heat settings allow you to customize just how warm your hands are (and the soft cotton material is extra cozy). However, we wish there were more camo patterns other than Realtree Edge. Not that the deer will notice or care, but some of us like our camo outfits to match.

Industry observers note that the Snow Deer gloves offer surprising dexterity for thicker gloves. They are suitable for everything from hunting to motorcycling thanks to the sheep leather palms that help provide additional grip. The heated wires in this pair of gloves extends completely to each of the fingers, making them a great option for anyone with arthritis or circulation problems in the hands. There is also fleece in the glove liners to help retain heat and repel moisture.

These gloves have a shorter battery life than some of the other options on this list. But they’re very well constructed. Features like the sheepskin palm and fleece lining add a lot of additional value for the money here. If you need gloves that are versatile for more than one outdoor activity, these are the ones to consider.

These featherweight gloves offer a great deal of dexterity that’s ideal for work or recreational activities in bitter cold conditions. The extra reinforcement of the palm and inside of the fingers further emphasizes the fact that these gloves are made with cold weather activities in mind. You can also cinch the cuff tight to prevent extra snow and wind from getting in at the wrists and dropping your core body temperature.

In a recent development, these heated gloves have a slightly shorter run time than we’d expect for a battery of this size. It runs for about two hours on high, three hours on medium, and five hours on low. Extra batteries are a necessity if you need them super toasty for long periods. That said, we think the shortened runtime is a decent tradeoff for the extra dexterity offered by these gloves.

It has been revealed that for the gloves I tested, I first made sure the batteries were fully charged. I then ran each pair on the highest warmth settings to assess the battery life of each glove. I also wore the gloves while performing a variety of activities both recreational and for work. This allowed me to evaluate the comfort and dexterity of each pair. Additionally, I considered the following factors when making my decisions:.

There are a few different types of heated gloves. The most popular style utilizes an electronic battery system and heated wires in the fabric, which is extremely effective for staying warm. The downside is that gloves like this are often expensive and require frequent recharging. Most have a battery life of six to eight hours depending on the set intensity level.

Recent findings suggest that there are also gloves and mittens with small pockets for chemical hand warmers. One pro to this style is the reduced cost. Of course, you can only use the disposable hand warmers once before tossing them in the trash. There’s also waste from the airtight wrappers this style of warmer is sealed inside, so it’s not exactly the greenest solution out there. But you don’t have to worry about charging any batteries and you can quickly replace the warmers in the field once they lose heat.

Sources indicate that when picking a glove, think about how you plan to use it. Thicker gloves are great if all you plan to do is ride a snowmobile or ATV. However, they can quickly become useless if you need to do more delicate tasks. Thick gloves can make it difficult to squeeze the trigger on a rifle or work on an engine. Think about dexterity and how much you’ll need. At the same time, be careful not to buy gloves that are too small or too tight.

For gloves that will be used primarily for working, it pays to go with thicker materials like leather that are built to take abuse. Ideally, the palms will be reinforced for heavier tasks like ranch work. It’s not a bad idea to go for work gloves that are waterproof—or at least water-resistant—either.

Industry observers note that many clothing manufacturers are now making their gloves with at least one specialized fingertip designed for operating a screen. The quality of these fingertips varies depending on the glove. Some gloves just don’t have the dexterity for typing or sending emails effectively. But quality ones make for great hunting gloves when you want to stay in touch with your buddies without losing any warmth.

Mittens are almost always warmer than gloves, and that includes heated mittens. This is simply because mittens allow your fingers to share warmth and slow heat loss. Of course, this comes at the cost of dexterity for more precise tasks.

Recent findings suggest that it can be a bit of a balancing act to find the right fit for warm gloves. Go with gloves that are too loose and you lose dexterity and warmth. If the gloves are too tight, they might cut off circulation. The ideal solution is to find gloves that fall somewhere in between. The gloves shouldn’t be so tight they feel restricting, but they also shouldn’t fall off your hands.

In a recent development, waterproof capabilities vary from glove to glove. Some have that feature built in standard while others may need to be kept out of the snow and ice to function properly. Be sure to read the fine print on any pair you buy first. Most work gloves are built rather ruggedly and will handle a little water.

Industry observers note that while the technology for heated gloves continues to improve, the Ororo gloves were a standout for us in terms of battery life. These large versatile gloves will get you through the worst sub-zero temperatures that nature can dish out, and the competitive price makes them a solid option for gearing up for another long winter. Even if you choose another pair on this list, the best heated gloves will keep your digits nice and warm all season long.

According to recent reports, but wait, there’s more: Another storm system is expected to move into the Sierra early next week, potentially bringing additional heavy snowfall just in time for Thanksgiving. Forecasts are calling for several more feet across the mountains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S. Senate Thursday night and now heads to the House.

The Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night. Support in the Senate eroded over the series of votes, from 73-25 on the first vote Nov. 9 to a final vote of 62-33. A bill requires a simple majority of 51 votes in the Senate to pass.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

BAAJA is co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from Latest Mexico often considered a conservation champion, and Sen. Mike Lee, the Utah Republican and architect of recent attempts to sell public land. Heinrich states BAAJA cuts red tape and will speed up renewable energy projects to help fight climate change, increase jobs, and bring down energy costs for average Americans.

Conservation advocates, however, fear it will also lock in projects many sportsmen and women have spent years fighting, like a copper-sulfide mine by the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the Pebble Mine in Alaska’s Bristol Bay. It also may well open the door for massive data centers on public land, something most of the conservation and sporting community resoundingly oppose.

Recent findings suggest that “I understand this is a massive, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life earlier this week.

Industry observers note that BAAJA proponents say it increases project certainty. Right now, one administration can reverse or cancel permits approved by a prior administration. But by limiting the back and forth between administrations the bill also drastically changes how much oversight a project can receive, even under foundational laws like the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act. The bill will also limit public input into projects and judicial overview.

Many of the nation’s tribes have forcefully spoken out against the bill saying it severely curtails tribal input.

In a recent development, “Overall, the bill, by weakening these bedrock laws, would make it far easier to fast-track AI data centers as well as fossil fuel, mining, and other extractive infrastructure. Once these projects are approved, they would be difficult to unwind,” according to the Western Environmental Law Center. “BAAJA would cause grave, generational harm to the West’s public lands, waters and wildlife, and communities.”.

Recent findings suggest that even conservation groups who support portions of the bill question how fast such a massive piece of legislation is moving through Congress. This is the first major permitting reform bill in decades and was introduced Sept. 30.

Read Next: Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Strategy Really Means for Outdoorsmen.

Recent findings suggest that the bill now heads to the House. If representatives make any changes to the Senate version, the Senate must vote again on the bill before it heads to President Trump’s desk for his signature. The president has remarked he supports the bill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southern Illinois school teacher Darin Hicks grew up in a hunting family, but he didn’t start hunting deer himself until just a few years ago. As his interest in deer hunting grew, he took special notice of any massive bucks he spotted during his daily drives to and from school as a science teacher.

Sources indicate that “I started seeing a large buck, but never in the day [at first],” the 40-year-old Illinois native tells Outdoor Life. “We don’t use trail cameras. But I got plenty of [phone] photos the last couple years of a really good buck — but only a few photos during the day.”.

Hicks was mentoring his 9-year-old daughter, Josie, who wanted her first deer to be a buck.

“I had her out in youth season, and she could have taken a lot of does but wanted a buck. One evening we saw a buck, but it was too dark [even though it was still legal light] and Josie didn’t want to shoot in that poor light.”.

Hicks thinks the buck that he and his daughter spotted that evening during the youth season may have been the giant buck he arrowed weeks later.

On Nov. 14 he hung a ladder stand near a wooded thicket full of rubs, scrapes, and plenty of trails. He set the stand for his dad, 77, to hunt during the upcoming Illinois gun opener on Nov. 20.

But that Saturday night Hicks’ wife, Katie, asked her husband if he wanted to bowhunt the stand the next day, before his father got in it the following week.

Sources indicate that hicks stated there wasn’t much time that next morning on Sunday before they left for church. Katie said he had a good two hours to hunt from dawn until leaving for church with his family.

She had a good point, Hicks decided, and climbed into the stand the following morning of Nov. 15.

He sat for about an hour and spotted a doe with twin fawns at 150 yards. Suddenly the doe with young spooked and out stepped the giant buck Hicks had seen from afar for the last two years.

In a recent development, “I was shaking, found my grunt call and blew it once,” he says. “He turned and started walking toward me and my heart was pounding overtime.”.

The buck came steadily closer while Hicks readied for a shot — the first time he would ever draw his bow on a whitetail.

“He walked toward me, stopped, and looked up at me at 15 yards, then he turned to head away,” Hicks says. “He started through some brush quartering away at 35 yards and I drew, released, and I heard a loud smack.”.

The buck collapsed in his tracks. Hicks’ arrow had hit a bit high, but his 2-blade mechanical struck the spine and the buck didn’t get up.

Industry observers note that hicks managed to wrestle the nontypical out of the woods and, field-dressed, it weighed 187 pounds. His taxidermist aged the buck at 5 1/2 years, with a gross green score of 226 1/8 inches.

Sources indicate that “We all still made it to church that morning,” Hicks says. “And I even got to teach Sunday School.”.

#21731. Why Hunting Mallards in Flooded Timber is So Great

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (918 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fieldandstream ↗ Open Full Page

Why Hunting Mallards in Flooded Timber is So Great

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply.
  • It can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control.
  • It has been revealed that two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply. A pair starts to circle, and that pair becomes four, then eight. Eight turn into 20. Somehow, the sight of ducks working over a timber hole draws more ducks from everywhere. It’s almost like squirrels running out onto branches to see what the others are chattering about.

It can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control. I’ve seen that in Arkansas, but we won’t see it here—in a duck-poor state a couple hundred miles north. The two dozen mallards wheeling over our heads are as good as it’s going to get. But from where we stand, pressed tight to the trees, two dozen is more than good enough. ­Editor-​in-​chief Colin Kearns and I are doing that thing where you look down but roll your eyes up, trying to peek at ducks without flaring them, and our hearts are beating fast.

It has been revealed that two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole. Travis Mueller, a Banded pro staffer, tells us not to shoot. He’s hoping the rest will follow. Kearns and I nod our heads—imperceptibly, we hope—and hold our guns ready. The rest of the ducks make one more circle, but higher and looser. Then they slide away. With the birds in the sky gone, we settle for the two in the bush. Jumping the two drakes, ­Kearns and I each shoot one. While we wish the rest had come in, the sight of these two in the trees, hanging over the decoys and lit by the morning sun, makes Kearns an instant convert to woods hunting.

Mueller, who scouts as hard as anyone, found this spot in spring by looking for beavers. Beavers plus woods equals flooded timber anywhere, and we’re standing in knee-deep water in the soft maples and willows growing between a couple of oxbow ponds. Mueller hunts here to get away from the crowds on the major water, but crowds have a habit of following successful hunters.

According to recent reports, the first rule of timber hunting: No one talks about timber hunting. Good hunters are secretive. Mueller is a great hunter, so it’s no surprise he’s long since crossed the line from secretive to completely paranoid. We left the ramp extra early this morning to avoid detection. Even so, Mueller fretted the whole way that a couple of kids he thinks are watching him might have found his spot.

Recent findings suggest that when we got to the hole, Mueller was sure his enemies were onto him. Three hundred mallards that had been sitting here yesterday weren’t here; someone must have run them out. And the decoys were missing—no doubt, in Mueller’s mind, stolen by the competition. As Kearns and I found fallen trunks for our gear, Mueller was looking for the bag of decoys he had stashed. We could hear him sloshing and cursing in the darkness.

In traditional flooded green timber, a lack of decoys wouldn’t be a problem. Old-school hunters in Arkansas relied on calling and ripples kicked in the water to attract ducks and went without decoys. Here, though, decoys and spinners are an advantage. There are no acorns to attract ducks. Birds don’t come to flooded soft woods to eat. They want a place to hide out and loaf. The ducks we’re after are trading back and forth between a couple of refuges, or coming back to the woods after feeding in the cornfields. They need enticement. In the words of a famous timber hunter: “There are two places you can kill a duck. Where he wants to be, and where he don’t mind goin’.” This is a don’t-mind-goin’ spot, hence, the need for decoys and spinners.

When Mueller finally shines his flashlight in the right place, he finds the decoy bag. The hole is still secret. In fact, we’ll see no other hunters nor hear any shots but our own this morning. Those 300 mallards? Who knows. They were probably fresh arrivals that dropped in, then found other ducks and relocated.

With two dozen decoys in the hole and four spinners going, we’re looking good. Spinners work well in the woods, Mueller believes, because ducks lose sight of them, then see them again, as they pass over the latticework of branches. And the sun is shining. “Sun’s out, guns out” is a truism of timber hunting. Decoys show up, spinners flash, and the sun creates shadows that make it easy to hide beside a tree.

Recent findings suggest that mueller blind-calls, quacking at random intervals to whom it may concern. Often in timber hunting, you don’t see the ducks you’re calling or decoying until after they have seen you. We’re not aware of the flock until we hear the whoosh of wings overhead. When the birds drop in I miss, Kearns kills a greenhead, and Mueller shoots a bluewing drake, fully plumed, unheard of at this latitude with 10 days left in the season. It’s been a strange migration year.

Industry observers note that we peck away at a few more, and call it a morning, being careful to pick up our hulls both because it’s what you do, and to hide any sign of our presence. For good measure, we pack the decoys out, too. A flooded hole in the woods is worth keeping secret.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • Sources indicate that after retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

Sources indicate that after retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

This interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Sources indicate that jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

It has been revealed that having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

Sources indicate that I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

Industry observers note that I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

And then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

Industry observers note that and so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a significant thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making fresh friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

No, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

Industry observers note that I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

It has been revealed that and so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Recent findings suggest that now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

Recent findings suggest that I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

In a recent development, while not a top pick in our recent shoe guide, we reviewed the Katana Lace in 2024 and called it an excellent shoe for edging and precision placements. It’s also great in narrow cracks and pockets. This is a good first performance shoe for the climber starting to think more about progression, and a great shoe for a climber who cares about performance, but doesn’t want an insanely uncomfortable pair to push their absolute limits. I’ve been climbing in the Katana since last winter and have found it a joy to wear in hand cracks, finger cracks, steep routes, and technical climbs with edging in the gym and on all types of rock. It’s not so great as a comfortable, all-day pair on moderates, or for slab, in my opinion.

Our favorite rope for trad climbing (as of fall 2026), the Black Diamond 9.4mm dry rope balances durability, sleekness, and light weight. During our testing process, we took substantial whippers, found ourselves hangdogging on steel permadraws, didn’t obsess over the dirt that got into our rope, and ran the 9.4 over grainy lips on sport pitches and across arêtes and edges on mixed and traditional pitches, as well. After months of testing, the rope barely showed any wear, which is notable for a 9.4 that feels skinny in hand and climbs as smooth and airy as an ultra-light—great for rope drag on monster sport climbs or zigzagging trad leads.

In a recent development, at the time of publication, only the 70m was in stock, with low inventory. If you’re climbing in low-moisture areas, you could get the same rope without the dry treatment (also 20% off), or save 20% on the 9.6mm version if you don’t mind the larger diameter (this version is a bit pricier because it’s bipatterned, making it easier to find the middle—worth the premium, in our opinion).

Recent findings suggest that our best all-around harness of fall 2026, the Black Diamond Solution uses what it calls Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. Our testers loved the contoured hip support and the durability of this harness. “I took hundreds of falls and [the Black Diamond Solution Guide] gets the highest praise I can give a harness, which is that I never even thought about my harness after a fall,” one of our testers mentioned.

Our top all-around men’s climbing pant of 2025, Black Diamond’s Alpine Light Pants feature a mobility-friendly design. We also selected them as our top women’s pick for trad climbing, multi-pitch routes, and alpine lines. While the Alpine Light pants are out of stock or low inventory right now, the Black Diamond Alpine Pants (which are, as you might expect, a bit less lightweight) are currently on sale. We found that this pant model struck an ideal balance between breathability while moving rapidly, and moderately protective in light winds and rain showers with its DWR coating.

In a recent development, one of our top mountaineering boots of the year, the G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.

In a recent development, in my humble opinion the Black Diamond Distance Carbon Z FKT Trekking Poles are hands-down the best trekking poles on the market. That’s thanks to the ingenious glove strap system that affixes to the pole with a magnet—no more faffing around trying to get your poles on and off with two hands. The gloves themselves provide excellent energy transfer, and the carbon poles are super light but also plenty sturdy. I used them for full 110-mile a lap of Mount Blanc this summer and they still look and feel as good as new.

It’s a tried and true staple for a reason. My footwork has never felt more precise than when I’m wearing the La Sportiva Bushido. That’s thanks to a specially-designed midsole that hugs your foot, Ghillie lacing, and an ultra grippy outsole. I, too, am now a proud owner of a pair and they nail the combination of comfort and style. I would most certainly wear them on a hike, and I also wore them to a wedding rehearsal dinner. The holiday season is meant to be a time to relax, be with friends and family, and, ideally, get some climbing in. Don’t let the obligation of holiday shopping take up too much of your time—the editors at Climbing have determined what we believe are the best gifts for the climber in your life, whether a gym, sport, trad, or ice climber, a burgeoning mountaineer, an all-arounder, or someone who hasn’t tried climbing yet, but is eager to get started.

Sources indicate that whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh new set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin. Fear not! Rhino Skin Solutions makes a purpose-built skin balm to restore your digits as efficiently as possible. Split+ is a roll-on cream that comes in two sizes (5oz and 3.4oz) and uses beeswax, vitamin E, arnica, dragon’s blood, and tea tree oil, offering a blend of occlusive (sealing) and antibacterial properties.

Sources indicate that ocun’s newly introduced Jett S climbing shoes are as comfortable as they are affordable, and best suited for the gym. They excel at precision placements and perform well on steep terrain, hooking, and scumming, on everything from 5.13 tech to the Tension Board 2 at 40° overhanging.

Last year, Petzl updated the Connect Adjust to make a good item great: they slimmed down the dynamic tether from 9.5mm to 9.0mm, making it noticeable lighter and easier to extend/contract. The belay-loop attachment point is now a sewn Dyneema webbing, rather than the thick rope itself, and as a result feels lower profile on the harness. The Connect Adjust also now features a pinhole to attach accessory cord to; if weighting the Connect, clip a carabiner into the accessory-cord loop and it will easily disengage.

Recent findings suggest that edelrid’s Ohmega brake assistant is a crucial belay tool for partnerships where the climber weighs significantly more than the belayer. By adding friction, the device makes the belayer “heavier,” reducing the size of whips and keeping the belayer on the ground during a fall. We recommend any climbing duo with a notable weight difference to invest in one.

Industry observers note that the Friend Camming Device is one of the most legendary and trusted pieces of climbing equipment. Newly updated for 2026, the Friends are a tiny bit lighter than the previous model, but, most importantly, they come with a new, seamless “Magic Cord” sling. The bartack-free sling enables smooth extension so you can enjoy your leads without rope drag.

Recent findings suggest that the Free Wall is the ultimate quiver-of-one backpack for rock climbers, made from a super-tough recycled nylon that our testers hauled for thousands of feet this summer. Unlike a traditional big-wall haulbag, with its simple, monolithic compartment, the Free Wall Pack is designed with on-the-wall access in mind: two internal pockets, two gear loops, and a large external pocket on top of the lid.

Apparently Scarpa’s Veloce is designed for beginner and intermediate climbers who spend all of their time at the gym—but our experienced field tester didn’t get the memo. After a quick break-in period, they became his go-to shoes inside and out, where he clipped the chains on the two hardest sport routes he’s sent in the last decade.

Black Diamond’s Magnetron has the smoothest operation of any triple-action carabiner we’ve ever encountered; a true one-handed operation that provides immediate security upon letting go of the gate. Its pear shape is ideal for belaying and rappelling, and it has a surprisingly narrow nose, making it easy to clip into chain anchors and busy masterpoints.

Recent findings suggest that these insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

According to recent reports, climbing tape isn’t just for hardcore climbers nursing a busted pulley or gobie—it’s a needed part of any decent first aid kit, repair kit, and can help you fashion a makeshift stickclip in a pinch. (BYOStick). Tension’s climbing tape is some of the stickiest we’ve used, performing well in both sweaty and freezing environments. The Tri-Pack includes a one-inch roll ideal for larger body parts like wrists and ankles and for making tape gloves should you forget yours at home, the half-inch roll works well for large blisters and flappers, and the 0.3-inch roll is preordained to fit individual digits.

What gift could be better than continued access to America’s best rock climbing? Gift your climbing partner a membership to Access Fund, the largest climbing advocacy movement in the country, which tirelessly protects and conserves historic areas—and opens latest ones. They’ll even get a free t-shirt.

Industry observers note that the daughter of Climbing’s editor in chief, Maya Silver, has worn the Black Diamond Momentum kids’ climbing shoe for the past four years. Once she finally outgrew it this last summer, the decision was easy to order her another pair. Like the adult Momentum shoe, the Momentum kids is super comfortable thanks to its neutral last, easy to get on/off with a simple Velcro closure, and offers sufficient performance for most little crushers.

Tech Report: Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Industry observers note that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that with all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

Sources indicate that with all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the major ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

Sources indicate that it’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

It has been revealed that unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Sources indicate that beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern Newly introduced Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Industry observers note that hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Major Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

It has been revealed that spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Massive Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

In a recent development, desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

According to recent reports, on long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries swiftly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

Sources indicate that my favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

#21722. Hannah Otto Broke Her Leg Descending Kilimanjaro—and Kept Riding

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1033 w)

Hannah Otto Broke Her Leg Descending Kilimanjaro—and Kept Riding

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hannah Otto celebrates at Uhuru Peak, the 19,341-foot summit of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, with her mountain bike.
  • By the time professional mountain biker Hannah Otto, 30, reached the final miles of her descent from Mount Kilimanjaro, 19,341 feet, she had already navigated the mountain’s most punishing terrain.
  • In a recent development, on November 3, Otto became the first known woman to ascend and descend Africa’s tallest mountain with a bicycle in a single day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hannah Otto celebrates at Uhuru Peak, the 19,341-foot summit of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, with her mountain bike. (Photo: Rachael Galipo).

By the time professional mountain biker Hannah Otto, 30, reached the final miles of her descent from Mount Kilimanjaro, 19,341 feet, she had already navigated the mountain’s most punishing terrain. She’d hauled her bike up snowy slopes, scrambled over boulders at 18,000 feet, and ridden steep, rocky trails where softball-sized stones shifted beneath her tires. Now she was on a rainforest dirt road easy enough to ride on a gravel bike.

In a recent development, on November 3, Otto became the first known woman to ascend and descend Africa’s tallest mountain with a bicycle in a single day. She completed the effort in 10 hours, 18 minutes, and 51 seconds, despite breaking her leg just two miles from the finish.

“I came around a gentle bend in the trail, and the trail went from dry dirt to mud, and it was like I hit ice,” Otto told Outside. “The bike just came out from underneath me, and I was on the ground in a second.”.

The fall had broken her leg. But two miles from the finish, she got back on her bike and rode out.

According to recent reports, the attempt was also part of a fundraising campaign for World Bicycle Relief, a nonprofit that provides bicycles to improve access to education, healthcare, and employment. Otto hopes to raise $165,000 to provide 1,000 bicycles to rural African communities.

Recent findings suggest that otto’s ride established the first known women’s time for a single-day bicycle ascent and descent of Kilimanjaro. Canadian mountain biker Cory Wallace completed an ascent and descent in 8 hours, 55 minutes in 2022, but no verified women’s time had been recorded before Otto’s attempt.

Otto, who has raced mountain bikes for 21 years, spent months preparing for the altitude and dramatic changes in terrain. Kilimanjaro rises through rainforest, heath and moorland, and alpine desert before reaching its snow-covered summit. Otto said temperatures ranged from about 70 degrees Fahrenheit near the base to 10 degrees near the top.

She trained as often as possible above 10,000 feet in Utah’s mountains, scheduled races at higher elevations, and added heat and sauna sessions to her routine. She also hiked on a steep treadmill with a sandbag on her back to train for carrying her bike.

According to recent reports, after seven days acclimatizing on Kilimanjaro, Otto returned to the base, rested a day, and started her single-day attempt at 3 a.m. with a support team that included her husband, a film crew, and local Tanzanian guides, aiming to beat the afternoon storm.

At about 15,500 feet, the terrain became too steep to pedal. Otto strapped her bike to her back and spent three and a half hours hiking three miles up snow-covered slopes approaching a 40 percent grade. Near 18,000 feet, she scrambled over large boulders with her hands, the bike still strapped to her back.

“With every 1,000 feet up the mountain, it felt like the bike gained five pounds,” she remarked.

Industry observers note that otto had planned three different ways to carry the bike, rotating between them for relief. Meanwhile, the altitude shortened her steps, raised her heart rate, and made every stumble harder to recover from.

Snow began falling just as she reached the summit. After hiking down the first steep section, she got back on her bike, thinking she’d beaten the worst of the weather. But rain had soaked the rainforest trails below.

After the crash, Otto tried twice to stand.

Sources indicate that “I watched my leg go in two completely different directions, and it was the most painful thing I’ve ever felt in my life,” Otto told Outside. “Both times, I fell to the ground screaming.”.

Recent findings suggest that her nearest guide was about 15 minutes behind her and could radio for a one-wheeled stretcher to carry her out. At first, she waited for help.

According to recent reports, but as she lay there, supine on the muddy floor of the Tanzanian rainforest, Otto told Outside that she imagined herself at 60, explaining that she’d been physically capable of finishing but had fallen short because of an accident. At the time, the thought made her sick. Living with that disappointment, she decided, would hurt worse than whatever her injured leg might put her through on the way down.

She army-crawled through the mud to retrieve her bike, used it as a crutch to stand, lowered the dropper seatpost, and draped her chest over the saddle to shimmy into a seated position.

Most of the remaining trail was downhill, allowing her to coast. Still, every bump sent pain through her broken leg. She used one hand to lift the injured leg onto the pedal for support, then moved it out of the way to pedal uphill with her good leg.

“There was also a piece of me that was riding out of fear and survival, even though it was excruciating,” Otto said.

When Otto finally reached the finish, about 20 Tanzanian team members sang, danced, and clapped as she approached. They knew she’d summited, but nobody had told them about the crash. As soon as they saw her condition, the celebration stopped.

Within minutes, the team had loaded her into a vehicle for the 45-minute drive over rough roads to the nearest hospital, where X-rays confirmed the break.

Rather than undergo surgery in Tanzania, Otto made the roughly 30-hour journey home with her broken leg. Back in Salt Lake City, she underwent surgery for two tibial plateau fractures and an associated ACL injury. She expects eight to ten weeks without putting weight on her leg, but hopes to return to racing in April 2027.

Despite the injury, Otto said the experience has changed how she thinks about her own abilities.

Recent findings suggest that “Now I feel like I have this story and this moment that I can always lean back on and be like, ‘You are so tough, Hannah,'” she said. “For me, that is the most reassuring thing that I could gift myself.”.

#21721. Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside.
  • Recent findings suggest that originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

In a recent development, audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing latest climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

“She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

Recent findings suggest that originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

Sources indicate that “With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” mentioned Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

Pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

“In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

Pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

#21720. 6 Forgotten Backpacking Skills Every Hiker Should Master

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1262 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

6 Forgotten Backpacking Skills Every Hiker Should Master

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, here at Backpacker, we respect old-school cool.
  • Calling the following six low-tech, high-technique skills “lost” might be a stretch—they definitely still have their fans, and every Backpacker editor has used them at least a few times.
  • In a recent development, whether they’re tying their tent’s guylines or their shoelaces, too many backpackers reach for the same overhand knot; it mostly works, but it lacks a certain… elegance?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Westend61/Getty Images).

In a recent development, here at Backpacker, we respect old-school cool. It’s not that we’re Luddites or avoid new ways of doing things—from lightweight internal-frame backpacks to gourmet freeze-dried meals, there’s no denying that most modern backpacking developments have made our experiences better. But there’s something about seeing a hiking buddy solve a problem with a retro skill that we admire. It demonstrates knowledge, competence, and the kind of self-reliance that every backpacker secretly aspires to.

Calling the following six low-tech, high-technique skills “lost” might be a stretch—they definitely still have their fans, and every Backpacker editor has used them at least a few times. But they aren’t part of the average beginner hiker’s repertoire anymore, and many hikers go their whole careers without using them. Start practicing them now to level up your skills for next season.

In a recent development, whether they’re tying their tent’s guylines or their shoelaces, too many backpackers reach for the same overhand knot; it mostly works, but it lacks a certain… elegance? While you don’t need a Boy Scout’s skill at knotcraft to go backpacking, learning to use the right knot for each job will help you finish camp setup rapidly and break it down without spending ten minutes coaxing apart the granny knot you’ve welded into your cord. Here are a couple to get you started (check out our guide to the 5 Essential Backpacking Knots for videos and in-depth descriptions):.

Slippery Backpacker’s Hitch: Good for hanging bear bags or rigging ridgelines for tarps, and comes undone with a pull. Wrap the rope at least three times around a tree or post, then tuck a bight of the loose end under the last loop.

Bowline Knot: A bombproof method for creating a strong loop. Make a loop in the rope; take the loose end and bring it up through the loop, around the rope, and back down through the loop. (You may or may not catch those of us who learned in school muttering “rabbit comes out of the hole, goes around the tree, and goes back in the hole” while we tie it.) Finish with an overhand and a half-hitch.

It has been revealed that sheet Bend: Need to attach two lengths of cord of different diameters? Create a bight with the bigger cord; bring the end of the thinner cord up through, wrap it around the back of the bight, and run it through the loop it creates.

Lightweight, direct-from-manufacturer shelters and quilts mean that there’s little practical reason to sew your own kit nowadays. However, for those who do like to get handy, the proliferation of patterns for sale and online tutorials on places like YouTube means that it’s never been easier to join the MYOG community. Plus, much like growing your own vegetables, sewing a few pieces yourself will give you a new appreciation for the ingenuity and labor that goes into making your gear.

Instead of jumping straight into the deep end with a high-investment piece like a tent or quilt, start small: A “ditty bag” is perfect for holding small items or replacing a torn or lost stuff sack. See our step-by-step instructions from our Spring 1973 issue, which is easy to sew without a machine. All you’ll need is ¾-yard of ripstop nylon, 30 inches of cord, needles, and thread.

Recent findings suggest that camp baking is everything modern backpacking meals aren’t: messy, ingredient-heavy, and slow. But there’s a kind of magic in coaxing a loaf of bread or a pizza into existence in the middle of the woods. It may not be an efficient way to eat, but it’s a rewarding skill, and as a party trick, guaranteed to impress your backcountry partners.

Industry observers note that the most traditional method is to bake in a Dutch oven using campfire. One easier and lighter way to start: Make a cupcake on your camp stove, which is satisfying and near-foolproof. You’ll need a single-wall steel or titanium mug, a pot significant enough to fit it inside, and a lid, plate, or aluminum foil to cover it. Empty a packet of microwaveable cake mix into the mug, add three tablespoons of water, and stir. Drop three small rocks into the bottom of your pot, balance the mug on top of them, and add enough water to the pot that it reaches the level of the cake mix. (If the mug starts to float, you’ve added too much.) Cover and simmer for 20 minutes, then enjoy straight out of the mug. Bonus: also works with pancake mix.

Even if most hikers have moved on to screened-in lightweight tents, flat tarps still have dedicated fans. Besides the unbeatably low weight, there’s a simplicity to making a shelter from a rectangle of fabric that we can still appreciate. (Looking for your first? Borah’s Silpoly Solo Tarps are solid, and at less than $90, eminently affordable.).

It has been revealed that there are innumerable ways to pitch a tarp, but the simple plow point shelter is a good place to start. Stake out three corners of your tarp, then use one of your trekking poles to raise the fourth, tensioning it with a guyline. (Pro tip: The first time you do this will take some trial and error to get a good pitch, so give yourself extra time in camp.) For extra dirtbag points, use a 9 x 10 scrap of Tyvek instead; create the guy-out points by pinching a bit of the material around a smooth pebble and tying off the base with a cord.

Recent findings suggest that whittling is one of those camp pastimes that’s largely fallen by the wayside—but to be fair, today’s backpackers are less likely than their predecessors to spend a lot of time kicking around camp. Still, basic knife skills are good to have in your pocket—you never know when you may need to carve a replacement for a snapped stake or shave tinder to build a fire—and whittling is a good, low-stakes way to practice those skills.

Carving a spoon is an easy project (and a useful one, if you forget your own utensil). Split a piece of deadfall, preferably still green. Carve your spoon’s outline, then hollow out the bowl. (You may have an easier time carving a shovel-shaped bowl than a traditional round one with a typical straight pocketknife.).

Industry observers note that once upon a time, planning a route for our magazine meant taking a walk down to the small library of guidebooks and topo maps we kept in the office and poring through them until we found the trail we were looking for. The world has changed since then—today’s mapping tools are quick and reliable for assembling a plan—but sketching out a trip the old-school way is still a good exercise for your brain. Plus, it can help prevent the kind of careless line-following that regularly gets hikers into trouble.

Recent findings suggest that picking up an expert-written guidebook for an area you blueprint on visiting regularly is always a good investment. Otherwise, the public library is your friend: Your local branch likely stocks an array of up-to-date guides, or can obtain them for you via interlibrary loan. Instead of carrying the whole thing, xerox the pages you need and jot points of interest and notes right on the copies. Pair with a compass and a current topo map (your library may stock those, too), and don’t forget to check with rangers or local hikers for the latest beta before you set out.

#21719. Industry News: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2686 w)
📖 Baca
