Industry News: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • In a recent development, directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Industry observers note that behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

In a recent development, directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Industry observers note that behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Recent findings suggest that posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

Recent findings suggest that when Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

Sources indicate that “My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he indicates. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

Recent findings suggest that “The rope would drop us off here,” he claims. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Recent findings suggest that infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he states, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

In a recent development, in a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees notes. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

Recent findings suggest that this was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

Industry observers note that “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

Industry observers note that scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza indicates, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Industry observers note that without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

In a recent development, while sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Sources indicate that over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

It has been revealed that while Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

According to recent reports, since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he claims. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

Sources indicate that since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he states. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I noted, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque indicates, “but mountain sports have not.”.

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque indicates.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque claims the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an key mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

Sources indicate that for all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he notes.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he states.

Newly introduced Research Shows Why Running Takes More Energy as We Get Older

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Normal wear and tear takes a toll, and your body needs more energy to cover the same distance.
  • A upcoming study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology in November 2026, found that some muscles in older runners were weaker than those in younger runners.
  • Sources indicate that “The aging process leads to decreased strength and volume of muscles, including the calf muscles involved in plantarflexion,” Changal T.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Running can get harder as you age. Normal wear and tear takes a toll, and your body needs more energy to cover the same distance.

A upcoming study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology in November 2026, found that some muscles in older runners were weaker than those in younger runners. Other muscles overcompensated for those weaknesses.

Sources indicate that “The aging process leads to decreased strength and volume of muscles, including the calf muscles involved in plantarflexion,” Changal T. Nguyen, MD, a sports medicine physiatrist, told Outside.

Dr. Nguyen is also a clinical assistant professor of orthopedic surgery at Stanford and was not involved in the study. “The calf muscles and Achilles tendon also become less stiff with age, so they work less effectively as a spring, she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that the good news, Dr. Nguyen said, is that adding a few simple exercises to your routine can help keep your calves strong and your Achilles tendon functioning well as you age.

The authors of the fresh study recruited 18 runners with an average age of 26.1 years and 18 runners with an average age of 63.4 years. The study referred to each group as “young athletes” and “master athletes,” respectively.

The researchers measured the athletes’ Achilles tendon stiffness and plantar flexor movements. (The plantar flexor muscles—located in the feet, ankles, and calves—propel you forward and upward as you run.) Then, both groups completed two six-minute treadmill sessions at two different speeds—roughly 5.6 miles per hour (mph) and 6.7 mph.

Sources indicate that they found that master athletes’ hips worked harder than those of younger athletes. Their ankles, on the other hand, did less work compared to those of younger athletes. Master athletes also exhibited weaker plantar flexors.

Some of these findings could be explained by decreased calf and Achilles stiffness, Dr. Nguyen remarked: “When the calf can no longer generate as much power at push-off, the body compensates by relying more on other muscles, such as those around the hip.”.

The researchers found that master athletes also spent more energy running, and their energy cost increased with speed.

“One notable finding is that the gap in energy cost widened at the faster speed, from about five percent to about 13 percent,” Dr. Nguyen stated. “This hints that the age-related deficit may grow as running demands increase, although the study tested only two moderate speeds, so whether the gap keeps widening at tempo or race pace is unknown.”.

It has been revealed that there are a couple of limitations worth noting. The study had a small sample size, and the runners were tested at only two speeds on a treadmill, Dr. Nguyen said. Because of these limitations, it’s uncertain whether the findings would hold in different settings—for instance, on a trail—or at different speeds.

Strengthening your calf muscles and improving Achilles tendon function promotes gait efficiency (the amount of energy needed to walk or run; a high gait efficiency means less energy is needed to complete the motions involved in walking or running), which can help you keep running as you age, Dr. Nguyen noted. She recommended three exercises that can help with this.

Sources indicate that if you’ve already taken a lap through our gift guide and still need more ideas, we’ve got you. All three of us editors here at Climbing have selected our top picks for gifts this year, from gear we’ve got our eyes on, to accessories in the climbing zeitgeist right now.

Sources indicate that some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your upcoming boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

In a recent development, originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

Having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

It’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk demonstrated how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

Recent findings suggest that luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:.

Shop Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

For climbers with pierced ears, a pair of carabiner earrings is a customizable accessory that never gets old. Recently, I’ve been getting tons of compliments on my pair of silver, locker draw earrings (yes, they actually screw and unscrew!) that I bought at the Yosemite Climbing Museum in July. You can buy them here, but stock is limited. In case they sell out, here are a few other great places to buy carabiner earrings online:.

After breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

The new Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. At an absurdly light 78 grams (2.7oz), the Alpha SL is for those going ultralight in the mountains, whether that’s an alpine rock romp or a big ski traverse. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

Shop Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness.

The Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

It has been revealed that the pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the latest film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

Have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

In a recent development, the oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

It has been revealed that note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a new collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

The trek over Auden’s Col in India’s Garhwal Himalayas is no stroll: Crossing the pass means working hard at elevations of up to 18,000 feet, crossing a glacier, and, occasionally, dealing with some of the world’s worst weather.

It was that last hazard that an expedition faced earlier this fall, when a freak snowstorm dropped more than six feet of powder on them with little notice. The 29-member team from Indian outfitter Aquaterra Adventures had reached base camp at 16,400 feet when the weather took a turn for the worse, battering them with heavy snowfall, temperatures down to -4 Fahrenheit, and 62-mile-per-hour winds.

It has been revealed that while Jetendra Singh Rana, their lead guide, rapidly called off their ascent and sent a message asking for rescue, the storm had flattened many of the group’s tents, leaving them all to squeeze into one remaining cook tent while they waited for help to come. Backpacker contributor Karthika Gupta spoke to expedition members to hear their story; read her full article and see footage from the  group’s ordeal here. –Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

In a recent development, on August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

Recent findings suggest that born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which rapidly became his true passion.

In a recent development, jun once said that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee notes that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

According to recent reports, jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and showed up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly released Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

Sources indicate that that was Jun—a man with an unbelievably big heart who was always looking for a way to help and who demonstrated up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

Jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”.

It has been revealed that climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

Tech Report: Boost the Performance of Your Canister Stove Without Blowing it Up

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed.
  • In a recent development, canister stoves, like the ones most backpackers use during the summer hiking season, perform poorly when the mercury drops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed. My fingers were chilled from fiddling with guylines, and I craved the feeling of a steaming cup cradled in my hands. I screwed my ultralight stove onto a fuel canister, squeezed some water from my filter bag into a pot, and lit up. And then I proceeded to wait for what felt like ages. The flame was low and weak. Had I packed a nearly empty canister? No. The feeble flame was a harbinger, much like the leaves littering the trail: Winter was coming.

In a recent development, canister stoves, like the ones most backpackers use during the summer hiking season, perform poorly when the mercury drops. Cold temperatures lower the internal pressure of the canister, causing it to falter, sputter, or produce a smaller flame. Regular winter campers often solve this problem by packing liquid fuel stoves like the MSR Whisperlite, which perform well in below freezing temperatures. Some canister stoves have a built-in pressure regulator that helps them stay efficient in the cold. But not every backpacker wants to shell out for an entire quiver of camp stoves. That’s where a little innovation comes in: Keeping a canister warm, even when the ambient temperature is frigid, helps maintain pressure so you can boil water on a regular canister stove all year round. Do it the wrong way, however and you might end up scorching more than your food.

When it comes to boosting the efficiency of your canister stove in winter, the key is gentle warming. A fuel canister’s contents are pressurized; when it is cold out, your goal is to increase that pressure ever so slightly. But overheating—and thus overpressurizing—can cause the canister to explode.

It has been revealed that warnings printed on the side of a canister tell this tale. Most manufacturers caution customers to keep a canister below 120°F. Heating a canister by rapid means, like placing it in boiling water is a very bad idea—just ask the guy who punched a hole in his ceiling trying to heat a canister for a fuel transfer.

How else can one warm a canister? One hiker on Reddit suggested sticking a chemical hand warmer next to the canister and enclosing it in an insulated pouch. But experts Backpacker spoke to did not recommend that method.

“You’re adding a continuous heat source while also insulating the canister, and there’s no particularly good way to monitor or control its temperature,” claims Adam Wilcox, senior mechanical design engineer at Jetboil.

Hothands, manufacturer of popular chemical warmers, claims that their products reach an average of 135°F, and warns that the maximum temperature can surpass 158°F. Granted, this doesn’t mean that placing a hand warmer beside your fuel canister will immediately warm the fuel contents to that same temperature, but it does heighten your risk of dangerously increasing  the pressure. Gentle warming is a safer bet.

Sources indicate that “Body heat before use or a controlled warm-water bath are much more predictable ways of warming a cold canister,” notes Wilcox. “The key with water is warm, not hot, and avoiding excessive heating of the canister.”.

For a quick boil, keeping the fuel canister inside your jacket for a few minutes prior to use may do the trick to increase internal pressure. Of course, the effects of this will diminish rather quickly as you run your stove and expose the canister to cold air. If you need to run your stove a little longer to cook a meal or melt snow, a warm water bath can provide safe, continuous warming. Place your fuel canister inside a dish or spare pot. (I like to carry a collapsible silicone bowl for this purpose.) Light your stove. As soon as the water begins to warm but before it boils, pour some into the dish surrounding your canister. You should immediately notice improved performance.

According to recent reports, shopping for a latest stove? Springing for one with a pressure regulator can help it perform more consistently across seasons. MSR claims that its Pocket Rocket Deluxe can run at full power at a fuel canister pressure of as little as 16.5 PSI. (A full canister would typically be at 45 PSI at room temperature.).

#21712. Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear.
  • Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

Industry observers note that for example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

Quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only enhancement is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

It has been revealed that if you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

It has been revealed that people in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

Get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-fresh isn’t always best.

Industry observers note that if you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Please keep reading, my opinions are notable. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

It has been revealed that A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

According to recent reports, this one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being said, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

Industry observers note that A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

Sources indicate that for headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

Sources indicate that for longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

The crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most important things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

According to recent reports, A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

It has been revealed that waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.

Supermoon Season Is Coming. Here’s Where to Watch in Every Single State.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, thanksgiving week will bring the first supermoon since January 2026. It kicks off a series of not one but four oversized full moons in a row, including the closest supermoon of the decade thus far in December. While you can admire the bright sphere throughout the night, a few specific tips and tricks will dramatically improve your view—including strategizing when and where to watch.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve chased at least a dozen supermoons as an astrophotographer and night-sky tourist, from the badlands of South Dakota to Serengeti National Park in Tanzania. In this guide, I’m sharing everything you need to know as we enter supermoon season, including timing logistics and guidance on where to watch the luminous sphere in every state.

The Thanksgiving-week supermoon will hit on Tuesday, November 24 It reaches full illumination that morning, but there’s an even better time to view it: sunset.

The round orb looks especially large and bright as it rises and sets due to an effect known as the moon illusion. A supermoon can appear up to 30 percent brighter and 14 percent bigger than the smallest full moon. Near the horizon, it looks even more gargantuan. If you’re hoping to snag supermoon photos, moonrise and moonset are the times to do it.

The full moon rises in the east to northeast as the sun sets in the west, and sinks in the west as the morning sun appears out east. The golden hour hues only add to the drama, turning the globe a tangerine tinge.

In a recent development, the last two supermoons of 2026 line up perfectly with holiday-season gatherings. In addition to a Thanksgiving-week event on November 24, we also have a full supermoon right before Christmas on December 23. It’s the closest full moon we’ve witnessed yet this decade, at 221,667 miles away.

After December, we have two more supermoons in early 2027: January 22 and February 20. You can use the following locations to watch these or any future supermoons, since moonrise and moonset locations remain relatively the same all year.

Industry observers note that while the supermoon looks stellar during both moonrise and moonset, I’m especially partial to its ascension because it doesn’t come with an early wake-up call. The full moon’s first appearance coincides with sunset. And soon after it rises, I can begin spotting a few constellations.

Sources indicate that with that in mind, here are the best places to watch the rising supermoon in every state. Remember: These locations are just starting points. You can absolutely watch the magic beyond this list. Just scout a viewpoint with relatively unobstructed vistas to the east, where the evening moon first reveals.

It has been revealed that pair supermoon watching with thick forest overlooks in Cheaha State Park, set 70 miles east of Birmingham. Out here, you can watch the crater-pocked orb rise from Alabama’s tallest point, Bunker Tower at around 2,400 feet. The simultaneously setting sun will turn the hardwood landscapes into varying shades of peach and pink.

Watch the supermoon ascend over mountain-flanked Kachemak Bay from the east-facing side of the Homer Spit, a thin sliver of land crossing 4.5 miles into the waterway. This glacier-carved landmass provides two-for-one awe; watch the sun set in the west and the moon rise out east. If you’re lucky, the northern lights could follow, too.

Catch the eye-popping supermoon rising above one of America’s most famed landmarks, the Grand Canyon. Mather Point’s east-facing view provides the perfect vantage point, although you’ll have numerous other lookouts to scout from, including Yaki Point and Shoshone Point, or further in the canyon along the South Rim trail. (Just read ahead on travel restrictions given recent flooding closures.).

In a recent development, head slightly west of Little Rock for one of Arkansas’ best supermoon viewpoints: Pinnacle Mountain State Park. The getaway’s visitor center is a popular spot for sunrise, which makes it great for moonrise, too.

In a recent development, death Valley is about as otherworldly as national parks get, even more so with a supersized moon rising above its surrounding peaks. Watch for the sphere above the badlands from Zabriskie Point, or head to Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes to marvel as it inches above the Grapevine peaks.

It has been revealed that perched above Boulder, the Colorado Chautauqua—a hub for arts, culture, and outdoor adventure—provides the perfect supermoon view. The earliest portion of the Chautauqua Trail, including the trail overlook, provides unobstructed glimpses to the east. For an easier vista, spot it right from Chautauqua Park. Don’t miss the sun setting behind the snowy Flatirons to the west, too.

Industry observers note that from Hammonasset Beach State Park’s boardwalk and shoreline, you can peer back and forth from the east’s supermoon to the west’s sunset, with the Long Island Sound in your foreground. Head to the park’s southern end, Meigs Point, for the most panoramic view. The beach is just over 20 miles east of New Haven.

The Point in Cape Henlopen State Park, where the Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic, offers another 360-degree supermoon and sunset perch. You can watch the moon crawl above the ocean as the sun dips beneath the bay and, if you situate yourself correctly (about one-third of the way up the west-side beach), behind the Delaware Breakwater East End Lighthouse. East-facing Rehoboth Beach just south of here is another stellar supermoon spot.

Barrier island Key Biscayne offers over a mile of east-facing beachfront perfect for catching the supermoon. Head to the Cape Florida Beach at Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park to enjoy it while watching for dolphins or visiting the Cape Florida Lighthouse; the park is within ten miles of downtown Miami.

For supermoon views with a surreal foreground, head to Jekyll Island’s east coast. Here, you’ll find Driftwood Beach, a waterfront made famous by its graveyard of gnarled oaks and pines. The lunar views continue down the coastline, including public access points like the South Dunes Picnic Area and Great Dunes Park. Or, join a Jekyll Island Dolphin Tour to swoon over the rising moon while scouting for cetaceans.

Industry observers note that with miles upon miles of scenic east-facing coastlines, the options for supermoon watching in Hawaii run the gamut. Try Pololū Valley on the Island of Hawaii for the chance to see our neighboring space rock as well as migrating whales, which visit the area from December to April. Catch it from the elevated overlook, or via a hike down to the waterfront.

In a recent development, for a sky-high vista, stroll the pedestrian sidewalks on Perrine Memorial Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho, just as the sun sets and the supermoon appears. Make sure to walk the east side to catch the lunar marvel above the Snake River, which runs over 1,000 miles from Wyoming to Washington state.

Downtown Chicago’s 18-mile lakefront pedestrian and bike trail is situated perfectly for a supermoon ascent. The route, located on the city’s east side, offers countless vantage points. Peer moonward from North Avenue Beach, the end of Navy Pier, or the viewpoint just behind Adler Planetarium.

According to recent reports, brown County State Park, nicknamed the Little Smokies, is the largest park in Indiana—and one of the best places in the state for seeing the supermoon. Drive up to the Hesitation Point overlook. It’s a local favorite for sunrise, which makes it perfect come supermoon season.

Stare slack-jawed as the supermoon rises above the Wisconsin River and the Mississippi from Pikes Peak State Park, one of Iowa’s best outdoor getaways. Viewpoints like the Pikes Peak Scenic Overlook are reachable by car, although you can get water-view hikes along the park’s 11.5 trail miles. It’s around 100 miles from Cedar Rapids.

In a recent development, the closer you can spot the supermoon to the horizon, the better, and Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve’s vast and flat fields do the trick. From the preserve’s scenic routes, such as Southwind Nature Trail, you can admire the lunar wonder along with potential bison, deer, and hare. The destination, part of the world’s largest remaining tallgrass prairie landscape, is 75 miles southwest of Topeka.

See the supermoon soar above the Appalachians from Pine Mountain State Resort Park in eastern Kentucky. The destination’s one-mile Chained Rock Trail leads you to a favorite local sunrise spot, gaining around 250 feet of elevation via stairs and packed dirt. Keep watch for wildlife like bears while you’re out here.

Any supermoon view will delight, but watching the orange orb reflect off water is especially enchanting. For that, try Louisiana’s Lake Martin, roughly 50 miles west of Baton Rouge. Fantastical cypress trees dot the water body, with frequent avian sightings from egrets to spoonbills. You can admire the scenery from the five-mile Levee Trail, or via kayak or boat.

Few coastal landmarks are as recognizable as Portland Head Light, a 1790s-era lighthouse perched atop Maine’s craggy coast. From here, sky-watchers can enjoy unobstructed views to the east—excellent for a sunrise or, soon, a supermoon. The lookout is six miles from downtown Portland.

From North Point State Park, you can watch the supermoon ascend above the country’s largest estuary, Chesapeake Bay. Get your legs moving on the park’s four-mile Hiker-Biker Trail, then watch the pockmarked moon appear from Crystal Pier or its adjacent beach.

Hear the crashing waves as you watch the peachy moon travel above the Atlantic. Halibut Point State Park provides a multisensory experience, complete with the scent of sea spray on the 440-million-year-old granite rocks. For the best viewpoint, head to the park’s northern tip, where you can look east to watch the supermoon and west to admire the plummeting sun.

Sources indicate that detroit’s 982-acre Belle Isle provides ample moon-viewing coordinates, all with the Detroit River as your backdrop. Hit the northeast section of the Belle Isle’s Driker Trail for the most unobstructed vista.

Recent findings suggest that perched atop a 130-foot cliff, Split Rock Lighthouse in northern Minnesota comes with serious supermoon potential—and, if you’re lucky, a chance to see the northern lights. To watch the moonrise down at lake level, make a detour to adjacent Pebble Beach.

In a recent development, sardis Lake, which is actually an over 98,000-acre reservoir set 60 miles south of Memphis, provides numerous supermoon vantage points. Watch the moon soar above this beloved fishing hole at the end of Pats Bluff or from the John W. Kyle State Park Campground.

See the supermoon’s first appearance from America’s smallest national park, Gateway Arch. This east-facing getaway has the perfect photo-composition recipe: if you’re standing in the right place (west of the arch), you can photograph the moon rising beneath the 630-foot colossus.

Visit the west side of glassy Flathead Lake to watch the lunar globe wow above the Mission Mountains. Stop-offs like West Shore, Substantial Arm, and Volunteer Park offer stunning vistas that are especially quiet come winter. If time allows, detour up to Glacier National Park just under 60 miles to the north.

Standing Bear Lake, located 20 miles from downtown Omaha, offers a unique urban vantage point on the roughly four-mile paved Standing Bear Lake Loop trail. Alternatively, try Omaha’s Glenn Cunningham Lake, with a variety of overlooks and campgrounds on the water body’s western side.

It has been revealed that head to the crimson crags of otherworldly Valley of Fire State Park. From the 1.5-mile Fire Wave Trail or the route’s scenic turnaround point, you can spot the supermoon above the sandstone. Other good moon-watching routes in this park, set around 50 miles from Las Vegas, include the Balanced Rock Trail and White Domes.

Sources indicate that upcoming Hampshire’s largest lake delivers a variety of supermoon vantage points. Try the Lincoln Park waterfront or the 1.5-mile route up Mount Major, a challenging ascent that leads to the 1,786-foot summit with granite balds and 360-degree views.

Pair the supermoon with the Statue of Liberty or Manhattan skyline for scale at Liberty State Park, one of Fresh Jersey’s most scenic public spaces. Hit the roughly two-mile waterfront walk for the best overlooks in this Jersey City park. It’s near the tail end of the 18-mile Hudson River Waterfront Walkway, which runs from the George Washington Bridge to Bayonne.

Sunset is one of White Sands National Park’s most popular moments, and for good reason. Golden hour turns this typically snow-white gypsum sand a mosaic of blush and tangerine hues. The landscape gets even more magical with a supermoon to top it off. You can catch the show throughout the dune system, particularly along the Alkali Flat Trail; just leave ample time to hike in and out, and note that the park closes 30 minutes after sunset.

Recent findings suggest that few destinations are as perfect for this winter’s two holiday supermoons as Lake Placid, particularly along the western side of Mirror Lake. The quaint mountain town goes all out with festive décor and winter fun, including bobsledding and ice skating. Meanwhile, you can see the supermoon reflect off of Mirror Lake from several overlooks, including Mid’s Park.

With its position along the Atlantic Coast, the Outer Banks boasts supermoon sightings galore. Hatteras Island wows with some of the area’s most impressive scenery, including the black-and-white-striped lighthouse circa 1870 and easily reachable beaches like Cape Point.

Theodore Roosevelt National Park is known for many things: its free-ranging bison, badlands scenery, and potential contiguous U.S. northern lights views. This winter, add a supermoon to the mix, particularly along the park’s scenic stop-offs like Badlands Overlook and Skyline Vista.

Ohio is another great place to pair lunar wonder with lighthouse explorations. Marblehead Lighthouse State Park, located right along Lake Erie, faces east for sunrise and, on lucky nights, a supermoon. This is the Great Lakes’ oldest continually operated lighthouse; it was first lit in 1822.

Industry observers note that visit the 2,500-acre Lake Hefner near Oklahoma City for supermoon wonder in the Sooner State. The Bert Cooper Trail loops you around the lake for roughly nine paved miles; the best lunar sightseeing awaits on the west side, including Lakeshore Park.

Industry observers note that the 16,000-square-foot Pittock Mansion brims with history, but that’s not all that’s on offer here. Pittock Mansion comes with one of the best views of Portland out to Mount Hood—all facing east. That means you could see the supermoon rising above the city, with the snowcapped 11,249-foot colossus in the distance. The grounds stay open into the evening, although mansion tours are limited to the daytime.

A hook of land juts out into Lake Erie from northern Pennsylvania, and it’s one of the state’s best spots for supermoon spotting. The getaway, Presque Isle State Park, is just four miles outside of downtown Erie. The National Natural Landmark comes with numerous east-facing vistas, from the sprawling beach to Gull Point Observation Deck (reachable via a 1.5-mile hike).

According to recent reports, many come to Newport for the Cliff Walk’s mansions, but the trail’s east-facing views promise incredible supermoon lookouts, too. Start at The Breakers and stroll north toward Forty Steps or beyond. You’ll have a number of views to choose from en route, not to mention a glimpse of the lives of Rhode Island’s rich and famous.

Recent findings suggest that for a South Carolina supermoon show, visit Folly Island, a roughly seven-mile barrier island that’s located about 10 miles outside of Charleston. The getaway’s public beaches make it easy to admire that scenic space rock. Try Folly Beach County Park for a land-based evening, or join a sunset boat tour from the island for the chance to see cetaceans beneath the shining orb.

Another otherworldly supermoon scene awaits in Badlands National Park. Stop-offs like Bigfoot Pass Overlook and Panorama Point look east across the park’s striated landscapes. Get a unique moon glimpse on the Door Trail, a short boardwalk that leads to a rugged and east-facing badlands hike with yellow posts to mark the way.

Sources indicate that the Kuwohi Observation Deck atop Great Smoky Mountains National Park offers a bird’s-eye view that’s spot-on for supermoon season. The only catch: You need to arrive early. This tower gets busy, particularly around golden hour. The road in also closes seasonally from December to March, so be prepared to hike if you’re coming for the later supermoons. Other options include the Newfound Gap parking area or the Gatlinburg Scenic Overlook just outside the park.

Scenic stop-offs abound along the 30-mile Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive in Substantial Bend National Park. Several offer great positioning for the supermoon to the northeast. Bookmark Blue Creek Trail, Sotol Vista Overlook, and the Goat Mountain Observation Point. For a near-private show, book a dome at stargazing retreat The Summit at Big Bend near Terlingua; guests can access a secluded hilltop complete with picnic tables, hammocks, and Chihuahuan Desert views.

With fewer crowds and flexibility to drive the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive generally between December and February, winter is one of the best seasons in Zion National Park. It’s even better when a supermoon’s on the horizon. Try Checkerboard Mesa pullout for some of the park’s clearest views to the northeast, or the paved Pa’rus for stellar scenery with the moon illuminating the canyon after it’s risen.

According to recent reports, find the supermoon rising above Malletts Bay from the three-mile Colchester Causeway. This serene perch is especially secluded in winter, as it’s not maintained for bikes. Instead, you can stroll it on foot from its starting point, Causeway Park, to soak up the scenery before driving back to Burlington, just nine miles away.

Sources indicate that admire the lunar sphere from Virginia Beach’s miles of sandy shoreline as it ascends over the Atlantic. Overlooks include Fort Story, home to the 157-foot-tall Cape Henry Lighthouse; Little Island Park from the Sandbridge Fishing Pier; or the Virginia Beach Oceanfront Boardwalk.

According to recent reports, rattlesnake Ledge in Washington’s Snoqualmie region is a favorite for sunrises, and the four-mile jaunt is just as impressive during supermoon season. From the peak, you can see Mount Washington, Mount Si, and the surrounding lakes. Expect fewer crowds than peak summer, but winter does bring the chance for ice and snow, so dress appropriately, especially when descending in the dark.

Industry observers note that west Virginia’s only national park brims with supermoon viewpoints. Chief among them is the Grandview Overlook, which peers across the Upcoming River’s horseshoe bend. Or get your heart pumping while chasing lunar wonder with a hike on the 2.4-mile Endless Wall Trail; make sure you reach Diamond Point Overlook by moonrise.

According to recent reports, spy the supermoon over Lake Michigan from many public waterfront lookouts in Sheboygan, nicknamed a freshwater surf capital of the world according to Livability.com. There’s North Point Park, kiteboarding haven Sheboygan Kite Beach, and the South Pier, which overlooks the Sheboygan Breakwater Lighthouse.

According to recent reports, the prairies stretch to the horizon in Thunder Basin National Grassland, an 875-square-mile ecosystem in northeast Wyoming. These endless views create the perfect recipe for supermoon views. Set trails are few and far between here—most visitors explore cross-country—but some hiking options include the East Upton Trailhead and Kellogg Trailhead in the grassland’s northeast corner.

#21710. How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life
