How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Recent findings suggest that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • Sources indicate that so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

Sources indicate that so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

These nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

If the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Sources indicate that challenges with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Sources indicate that firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “blueprint falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

Industry observers note that what if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

Recent findings suggest that if pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

It has been revealed that the boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

For maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

According to recent reports, an alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

If it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

It has been revealed that sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

The biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Industry observers note that many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

In a recent development, the most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

Recent findings suggest that the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

It has been revealed that if those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

In a recent development, once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

The lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

Recent findings suggest that now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

If the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

Recent findings suggest that if you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid big swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

Recent findings suggest that if a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

On coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

Industry observers note that with both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done swiftly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

Technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a significant, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

There are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

Recent findings suggest that lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is crucial.

Lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

But, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the concern being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

Recent findings suggest that if you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

But what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

Sources indicate that while you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a new stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

According to recent reports, but what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is important. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

In a recent development, lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

If the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

If the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

Industry observers note that however, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

In a recent development, speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

It has been revealed that the climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

Industry observers note that see? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m.
  • It has been revealed that in just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns.
  • Sources indicate that “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 upgrade on the floods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28 and the Continental Divide Trail.

It has been revealed that in just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

Sources indicate that “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 upgrade on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”.

Sources indicate that as many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A video posted to Instagram highlights the Junction Creek trailhead sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

“Junction Creek Trail #553 suffered a near-total loss in places where it parallels and crosses Junction Creek,” a USFS conditions report from November 13 reads. “Miles of trail as well as multiple bridges crossing Junction Creek were wiped out, replaced with massive piles of boulders, trees, and other flood debris.”.

According to the report, both the lowest trail bridge at 2.6 miles from the trailhead and the Walls Gulch Trail Bridge at 14.6 miles were destroyed. One social media video shows the first footbridge washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote.

According to recent reports, in an interview with The Gazette, Talley remarked, “The Colorado Trail Foundation has never experienced an event that damaged this much trail. This is the largest section of trail ever damaged in our 52 years.”.

Authorities claim that recovery work will likely begin in spring and carry into summer 2027 due to weather. They discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

Sources indicate that “Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” a USDA Forest Service Facebook post reads. “Don’t become a statistic—rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”.

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate aims to avoid the area.”.

Recent findings suggest that on November 2, the CDTC posted another upgrade for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it stated. While the interactive map on its website highlights no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”.

Outside of Colorado, New Mexico also experienced severe flooding. However, Audra Labert with the CDTC told Backpacker, “The area of New Mexico near the southern terminus did not experience significant damage from flooding.”.

Recent findings suggest that while the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

In a recent development, “While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”.

A Teen Hiker Needed Rescue on a Popular Tahoe Peak. An Expert Explains Why Snow Makes It Dangerous.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, el Dorado County Search and Rescue volunteers search snow-covered terrain on Mount Tallac near Lake Tahoe during an overnight operation to locate a missing 17-year-old hiker.
  • Search and rescue volunteers saved a 17-year-old hiker missing on California’s Mount Tallac on November 16 after following bootprints through the snow for hours.
  • The teenager, whose name authorities have not released, revealed early signs of hypothermia when responders found him in rugged terrain away from the established hiking trail, the El Dorado County Sheriff’s Office wrote in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, el Dorado County Search and Rescue volunteers search snow-covered terrain on Mount Tallac near Lake Tahoe during an overnight operation to locate a missing 17-year-old hiker. (Photo: El Dorado County Sheriff's Office).

Search and rescue volunteers saved a 17-year-old hiker missing on California’s Mount Tallac on November 16 after following bootprints through the snow for hours.

The teenager, whose name authorities have not released, revealed early signs of hypothermia when responders found him in rugged terrain away from the established hiking trail, the El Dorado County Sheriff’s Office wrote in a statement.

In a recent development, “The Sheriff’s Office is grateful that this search and rescue effort had a positive outcome,” the agency wrote. “However, situations like this can swiftly turn tragic, particularly in challenging winter conditions.”.

Industry observers note that located near South Lake Tahoe, Mount Tallac reaches an elevation of 9,739 feet. And in November, high-elevation conditions can deteriorate rapidly.

“In inclement weather, especially later in the day when it starts getting dark, it’s tough to find your way if you don’t already know the terrain,” Jared Manninen, a local outdoor writer and founder of the website Tahoe Trail Guide, told Outside.

Mount Tallac is one of the most popular summit hikes in Lake Tahoe’s Desolation Wilderness, a nearly 64,000-acre expanse of federally protected backcountry in the Sierra Nevada, but it also draws search-and-rescue calls year after year. The ten-mile trail climbs roughly 3,500 feet through steep, rocky terrain that becomes especially difficult to navigate once snow covers the route.

Even on a well-traveled route like the Mount Tallac Trail, a few inches of snow can make the trail much harder to find, especially on the descent.

The teenager was hiking alone on November 15, texting his family as he descended. When his messages stopped around 5 P.M., his family contacted the El Dorado County Sheriff’s Office within two hours. Recent storms deposited six inches of snow on the mountain, and forecasts called for additional snowfall, high winds, and reduced visibility.

Using the teen’s last known coordinates from his emergency locator beacon, rescuers narrowed their search to a rugged area of Mount Tallac known as The Bowl, a sweeping, boulder-filled basin along the hiking route just below the mountain’s upper ridge.

Recent findings suggest that A Washoe County Sheriff’s Office helicopter initially searched from the air but called off the search because of worsening weather. El Dorado County Search and Rescue volunteers continued on foot toward The Bowl, where they found bootprints in the snow.

Sources indicate that after following the tracks for several hours, rescuers located the teenager around 1:30 A.M. northwest of Floating Island Lake, a small alpine lake along the lower section of the trail.

Responders treated the hiker’s cold-related injuries and escorted him back to the trailhead, where he reunited with his family.

Despite its popularity, Manninen noted that the route up Mount Tallac is far from easy.

“It’s a quintessential hike because it’s so iconic,” Manninen stated. “You have such amazing views, but again, it’s a legitimate hike. It’s a significant commitment.”.

Manninen described The Bowl as a steep, open slope of loose granite and boulders above a small alpine lake along the summit trail. In summer, the trail is fairly easy to follow, although the loose rock can make for slow going. But even a few inches of snow can hide the route, and hikers can’t always count on following their own footprints back down if more snow falls.

In a recent development, according to local news outlet South Tahoe Now, a similar rescue unfolded on Mount Tallac in November 2024, when search-and-rescue volunteers followed tracks through the snow to find a lost hiker who couldn’t find his way down. Rescuers reached him around 4 A.M. and escorted him down a longer, less hazardous route.

In October 2017, responders rescued a stranded couple who became disoriented after coming across patches of snow left by an earlier storm along Mount Tallac’s eastern slope.

It has been revealed that for anyone planning to hike Mount Tallac in snowy conditions, Manninen recommended starting early, bringing a partner, studying the route beforehand, and carrying a paper map rather than relying solely on electronic navigation. He also advised packing a headlamp and extra layers in case the hike takes longer than expected, or otherwise choosing a different trail when the weather isn’t cooperating.

“It does seem like every year we have at least one person, couple, or group that ends up getting turned around on Mount Tallac and needs some type of rescue,” Manninen remarked. “It’s just a tough mountain.”.

The El Dorado County Sheriff’s Office reminds hikers to stay on established trails and carry enough gear to spend an unexpected night outdoors.

Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • Sources indicate that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • It has been revealed that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Sources indicate that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

It has been revealed that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing massive things.”.

Actually, substantial is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a newly introduced best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

According to recent reports, “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a big challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

The setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

“I just set it and left it,” she said. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

In a recent development, “I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she mentioned. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

Her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

Sources indicate that “As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she said. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

She never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

In a recent development, “I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she said. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

It has been revealed that the temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Industry observers note that working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

In a recent development, “I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she said of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Recent findings suggest that instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

It has been revealed that the aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

Industry observers note that “There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

As Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she stated.

Sources indicate that beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

Recent findings suggest that and in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

In a recent development, “I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case mentioned. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

#21706. Industry News: On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (857 w)

Industry News: On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • According to recent reports, there is a cinema up north.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a film review of sorts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

According to recent reports, there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

Recent findings suggest that this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

According to recent reports, I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

According to recent reports, however, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a massive-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

I watched The Alpinist on the major screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

According to recent reports, nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

L.L. Bean Pathfinder BOA Rec Snowshoe Package.

Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes.

Sources indicate that after a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip. Looking for a crazy-affordable pair that will last for years? The Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes ($50-70) are nearly bulletproof, easy to manipulate with gloves on, and provide a full feature set. This year we added the L.L. Bean Pathfinder Snowshoe Package (Best Snowshoe Package) and Atlas Montane ($250) (Best for Deep Snow.).

Snowshoes are some of the oldest winter gear known to humankind—the tech literally has prehistoric origins, with rudimentary versions dating back nearly 6,000 years ago. Today, the top ‘shoes boost flotation, grip, and ease of use, all while shaving weight. Over the years, our testers have tried hundreds of models in waist-deep drifts, through wet, cement-like snow, and on steep, icy slopes, all in the name of narrowing down the top of the class. Here are the best snowshoes of 2027.

Sizes: 22, 25 in Weight: Men’s: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4.1 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 3.6 lbs (22 in), 3.9 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: Men’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 220 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 lbs (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Easy-to-engage heel lift + Very secure binding – Pricey.

In a recent development, the Revo Explore snowshoes from MSR have been a tester favorite for over a decade: They’re lighter, more flexible, and grippier than most snowshoes on the market today. Credit a hybrid construction, which combines a tough, injection-molded plastic decking with a jagged-edged steel frame and pivoting toe crampon. The 2026 model keeps last year’s new binding—the TPU rubber stretch mesh Paradigm—which continues to impress testers with its security and comfort. The ridged, steel frame boosts side traction, while the two front toe crampons and a small, tooth-lined crossbar provide enough bite to stick to icy hills and steep ravines. Our Oregon tester reached for them in everything from deep powder to spring crust in Eastern Oregon’s Wallowa and Blue Mountains—when other people weren’t using them. “My husband makes fun of snowshoeing (he’s a skier) and claims to hate it, but I caught him happily using this pair,” she said.

Sizes: 20.5, 22.5, 26.5 in Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5), 3.8 lbs (22.5), 4lbs (26.5) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (22.5 in), 300 lbs (26.5 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent grip + Comfortable stride + Tall heel lift – Expensive.

According to recent reports, the Highlander Instinct takes the snowshoe crampon and dials it up to 11. Most snowshoes have a basic underfoot crampon for some traction on slopes, and a few brands add teeth around the edges. The Highlander Instinct uses a stainless steel crampon under the toe that’s as long and sharp as some mountaineering crampons we’ve used, plus lateral grips around the edge of the chassis and mini serrated grip bars at strategic grip points across the platform. Over three days of steep, icy hills in Rocky Mountain National Park, our tester didn’t slip once, aided, in part, by the easy-to-use heel lifts. The rockered profile and wasp-waist shape allow a natural stride and help the crampons bite, no matter the incline. That narrow waist and tapered tail kept these easy to walk in, too, without the waddling common in most wider snowshoes. They floated well in a few inches of latest snow, but drifts of more than a foot proved challenging. The BOA bindings were easy to adjust even with bulky gloves, and once dialed in proved extremely comfortable and secure.

Sizes: 25, 30, 36 in. (men’s) 21, 25 (women’s) Weight: 4.9 lbs (25 in), 5.6 lbs (30 in), 6.5 lbs (36 in) Maximum Load: 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 280 lbs (36 in).

Pros and Cons + Great traction on hills + Easy to adjust, glove-friendly binding + Wide range of sizes – Wider decks can be cumbersome.

Industry observers note that L.L. Bean’s Pathfinder snowshoe package impressed beginners and experts alike among this year’s Rocky Mountain test team. The BOA bindings—not often found in beginner-friendly packages—were a fan favorite, snugging promptly over mountaineering boots and casual snowboots and never needing another adjustment. The bindings were easy to use while wearing gloves and mittens, a big plus on a trip to Rocky Mountain National Park’s Emerald Lake where the windchill dropped to -20 degrees.

Industry observers note that on a windy, late-season day in the Indian Peaks, the crampons easily bit into steep ice crust in the morning, and the decks—made of high-density polyethylene—floated over thick corn snow in the afternoon. The poles are sturdy aluminum and adjust with an external lever lock that never failed or stuck. The only con was the width of the frame, which occasionally snagged on willow tips and low-hanging branches. But once in the open powder above treeline, the wider area underfoot became a plus. If you want a sturdy set of snowshoes and poles that holds up in most winter conditions, the Pathfinder Package delivers.

Sizes: 22, 25 in. Weight: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Good traction on slopes + Easy-to-use binding + Heel lift – Expensive.

It has been revealed that many snowshoes are unisex, which means they tend to be too massive for lighter folks who don’t need the oversized frame. The women’s-specific Lightning Ascents are nearly an inch narrower and five ounces lighter than the men’s version, making them perfect for smaller people with narrow gaits. The Ascent’s binding, a comfortable rubber mesh toe cup that secures via two rubber side straps that buckle into place, is simple to use with just a quick two-handed pull. The tooth-lined stainless steel frame and pivoting, two-pronged toe crampons impressed on outings in Rocky Mountain National Park’s Glacier Gorge, where our 5’4”, 115-pound tester tackled icy sidehills and slippery windcrust. But the Lightning Ascent isn’t just ideal for smaller snowshoers: Our 5’10”, 155-pound tester also found the precise, narrow ‘shoe design useful while climbing the gullied slopes of northern Vermont.

Recent findings suggest that sizes: 20.5, 23.5, 27 in. Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5 in), 3.8 lbs (23.5 in), 4 lbs (27 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (23.5 in), 300 lbs (27 in).

Pros and Cons + Intuitive BOA system + Multi-direction crampons + Flexible + Heel lift – Expensive – No tail extensions – Not great in powder.

For those who loathe fiddly snowshoe bindings, the Symbioz Hyperflex Instinct is a godsend. While several snowshoes incorporate BOA closures into their design, few are quite as simple as the Instinct’s. The design: a single knob that tightens the toe, sides, and heel using interlinked cables that run through the perimeter of the binding, eliminating any and all trailhead exasperation. It takes fewer than 10 seconds to step into and secure the snowshoe, but the Instinct stayed glued to our boots all day long, even while walking on bumpy, uneven terrain in Colorado’s Indian Peaks Wilderness. Another characteristic we loved: flexible decking made of injection-molded polypropylene. The pliable material gave us just enough torsional flexibility to enhance comfort and reduce ankle-twisting on uneven surfaces. While sidehilling through a labyrinth of postholes in Rocky Mountain National Park, eight lateral stainless steel teeth kept our Colorado tester upright and stable.

Size: 25 in Weight: 2.2 lbs (Tru Trak bindings), 2.4 lbs (Spin Bindings) Maximum Load: 215 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Easy-to-use BOA-style bindings – Below-average traction – No heel lift.

Over a pound lighter than the next-lightest snowshoes in our test, the Elite Race Ultralights, designed for endurance and adventure races, delivered on their name. Even with ultralight bindings and minimalist crampons, these snowshoes impressed testers with their durability. The PU-coated nylon mesh decking and aluminum alloy frame stood up to rock-studded snow slopes and scraped across ice with barely any sign of wear. Our testers loved them for their comfort and ease of use; thick foam padding around the binding straps eliminated hot spots, and once set, they stayed on without further adjustment. The narrow tails let you walk—or run—with your normal stride. One tester taught several Avalanche Terrain Avoidance classes for the Colorado Mountain Club in these snowshoes, where their ease of use and float in five inches of fresh snow was the envy of all her students. There is a cost to mild crampons and the simple plastic ridges on the perimeter frame: The Ultralights gripped well on moderate slopes, but skidded a bit on steep ice.

Recent findings suggest that sizes: 21, 25, and 30 in. Weight: 4 lbs (21 in), 4.2 lbs (25 in), 4.8 lbs (30 in) Maximum Load: 120-250 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Very affordable + Convenient, effective heel lift + Glove-friendly bindings – Heavy.

The updated version of our perennial budget pick, the Retrospec Drifter, impressed with good flotation, comfortable heel lifts for hills, and glove-friendly bindings.

The double ratchet strap bindings proved secure, intuitive, and easy to adjust, with buckles that were large enough to be manipulated without removing our gloves. The heel lift was ideal for 30-degree slopes in Rocky Mountain National Park, and was much easier to flip up or down—even with gloves on—than last year’s model. For a shoe that costs less than a quarter of some of our other winners, that’s an impressive feature set.

Plus, the Drifter is just about as bulletproof as a snowshoe gets: The one-piece polypropylene deck and aluminum alloy frame didn’t show a scratch from early-season rocks, surprise tree roots, and a long rattly drive in a roof box full of pointy gear.

Our Colorado testers found the underfoot crampons perfect for hard snow in the Indian Peaks, but with only six main crampons beneath the toes and no teeth around the perimeter, anything steeper than a 20-degree slope felt pretty sketchy when iced over. The Drifters also aren’t particularly strong in the flotation department: Our five-foot-four tester, who used the shorter 21-inch version, struggled to stay afloat the most.

But for $50, these snowshoes pack plenty of great features into an adventure-ready, accessible package.

Size: 22 in Weight: 3.6 lbs Maximum Load: 180 lbs.

Pros and Cons + One size fits all + Affordable + Impressive traction + Float tail-compatible – No heel lift.

In a recent development, described by testers as “aggressively sturdy,” these near-unbreakable injection-molded snowshoes will get you where you want to go with minimal fuss and fear of equipment failure. The stiff plastic body doesn’t have a lot of flex to match a hiker’s gait, but was ideal for packing down the trail for our Oregon-based tester’s three adventuring huskies.

Recent findings suggest that the Evo Trail’s serrated steel traction rails, four-toothed toe crampons, and plastic, anti-slide ridges kept our testers upright, even on crusty sidehills. Flotation is great, too, for such a small snowshoe. One of our Pacific Northwest-based testers took the Evo Trails through 20 miles of deep, unconsolidated snow in Oregon’s Blue Mountains and stayed on top of the powder the entire time—no easy feat in the chilly, snowbound region.

This year’s model uses the brand’s Paraglide binding, which combines a wide piece of stretch mesh over the toe with a simple heel strap. They climb decently well without a heel lift, though we think it should be a standard feature, even on this entry-level ‘shoe.

Sizes: 23, 27 in (women’s), 25, 30, 35 in (men’s) Weight: 4.3 lbs (25 in), 4.7 lbs (30 in), 5 lbs (35 in) Maximum Load: 160 lbs (23 in), 200 lbs (27 in), 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 300+ lbs (35 in).

Pros and Cons + Great float + Heel lift + Good traction on hills – Bindings can be fiddly.

According to recent reports, the Atlas Montane’s lightweight PVC decking and an aluminum tube frame combine for a classic deep-powder snowshoe. Our six-foot-two, 200-pound Colorado tester took the 30-inch version for a winter ascent of Longs Peak and floated easily over two to three feet of upcoming snow, even with a pack full of heavy climbing gear. Even the smaller decks (down to 23 inches) wowed our testers with easy traverses of powdery alpine meadows and serious forest drifts. Underfoot crampons and carbon steel lateral grips at the snowshoe’s midpoint kept footing sure and steady even on icy sidehills.

It has been revealed that the Montane is wider than most of the other snowshoes we tested in both the men’s and women’s models, which gives this ‘shoe its superior flotation, but it does take a moment to adapt your gait and stop banging the snowshoes together. Our testers found the strap bindings fiddly with thick ski gloves on, but once the two straps were latched in place, they stayed there for the whole trip. On powder days, the flotation more than makes up for the simple, slightly inconvenient binding. If you’re planning off-trail travel in deep snow, especially if you’ll be carrying heavy overnight packs, these are the snowshoes for you.

Flat, uncomplicated terrain doesn’t require too much from a pair of snowshoes. Simple, comfortable bindings and a deck that provides adequate flotation are all you need. If icy slopes or deep snow aren’t in your future, save money with a budget pair made from heavier molded plastic and less aggressive traction.

On the other end of the spectrum are snowshoes built for challenging terrain—slushy hills, narrow singletrack, or mixed rock and ice. A secure wrap around the heel and/or multiple straps along the foot are crucial for stability. Quick binding systems, like those that utilize a BOA twist lock, are helpful when taking snowshoes on and off in precarious terrain and a huge time-saver compared with fiddly three-strap setups. Snowshoes geared towards mountainous ascents will have a wider variety of spikes and crampons underfoot—and in more abundance—to offer grip both horizontally and laterally, and to bite through different types of ice. A heel lift that provides about 2 inches of lift (that’s easy to flick open and closed with either gloved hands or a trekking pole) is a must for giving your feet and calves an assist on the steeps.

In deep, fresh powder, you’ll want wider, longer snowshoes (or those that come with extensions) for superior flotation. On the flipside, if you’re headed out on a weight-conscious backpacking trip and/or initiative to strap the snowshoes to your pack for much of the trip, prioritize lightweight construction, like a pair made from aluminum and TPU-coated nylon, for reducing fatigue on-foot and outside your pack.

Sources indicate that over the past several years, our veteran testers braved blizzards, sub-zero temps, and icy alpine climbs to find out which snowshoes are really the best. Only nine models stood up to the rigors of our testing to earn a spot on this list.

Industry observers note that we looked at design, features, ease of use, comfort, traction, cost, weight, and flotation in deep snow to narrow down the best of the best from the current market. This year, some tried-and-tested snowshoe models received updates, like newly introduced bindings and decking materials, which we then reevaluated. Others haven’t changed through the years: their simple designs and technologies have withstood the test of time.

Industry observers note that kristin Smith A former Backpacker editor, category manager Kristin Smith has been a full- or part-time mountain guide for most of the last decade. In her spare time, she teaches Avalanche Terrain Avoidance for the Colorado Mountain Club, guides clients through the nearby peaks of Rocky Mountain National Park, and maps out new places to visit with her recently-acquired pilot’s license.

Jill Yarger Jill Yarger works as a mountain guide in Boulder, Colorado. She moved for an engineering job, found the mountains, and never left; that was almost 40 years ago. Since then she’s spent 13 years volunteering in the Rocky Mountain Rescue Group, joined the National Ski Patrol and Mountain Rescue Associations, and climbed in Alaska, Italy, and Canada.

Recent findings suggest that jessica Bucklin Jessica Bucklin spent a decade sailing tall ships all over the world before moving to the coast of Maine, where finding enough snow to snowshoe often requires just a walk down the road. When she’s not exploring Maine’s mountain parks she captains a towboat out of Bath.

Joe O’Leary Joe’s guiding career spanned North, Central, and South America before he settled in Colorado, where he now trains other guides in whitewater rafting, mountain biking, backpacking, and leadership development. When he’s not biking, rafting, or kayaking, he works as a nature photographer and writer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kayaking is among the outdoor recreation activities available in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Mount Kalaga National Park, where players can paddle along wooded waterways.

Many gamers have waited 13 years for a latest Grand Theft Auto (GTA)  game so they can steal cars, rob banks, and wreak havoc in a fictional American city. I had a slightly different mission. I wanted to go hiking.

In a recent development, GTA VI, the long-awaited installment in Rockstar Games’ blockbuster franchise, arrived November 19 with an enormous open world set in Leonida, a fictional state modeled after Florida. Beyond the game’s cities and beaches are mangrove swamps, forested mountains, and a surprising number of opportunities for outdoor recreation.

Among them is an entire national park that some fans believe was inspired by Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park. Naturally, as a journalist who covers the outdoors, I decided to investigate.

Sources indicate that getting there was its own expedition. I spent several hundred dollars on a PlayStation 5 specifically for this assignment, endured a download that initially threatened to take 14 hours, and worked through introductory missions involving a robbery and a dubious boating operation before I could drive north to the game’s national park—Mount Kalaga.

Sources indicate that located near Leonida’s northern border, Mount Kalaga is one of six major regions players can explore, with a vast stretch of mountainous backcountry offering hunting, fishing, and off-road trails, according to Rockstar’s official description. It took me about 20 minutes of real-life driving to get there from the game’s starting point, though my tendency to crash into medians at full speed probably added a few minutes to the trip.

Mount Kalaga isn’t especially faithful to real-world park rules. Hunting is generally prohibited in U.S. national parks unless specifically authorized, while off-road vehicle use is restricted. Still, the park’s layout, scenery, and recreation options reflect an impressive effort to make the fictional outdoors feel like somewhere worth visiting.

The drive into the park looks a lot like Northern California, with winding roads cutting through steep, lush hillsides. Farther in, the landscape opens up to waterfalls, rocky cliffs, and wide waterways bordered by dense vegetation, with forested islands and bridges stretching across the valleys below.

In a recent development, more impressive than the landscape was how well the game designers captured the everyday details of an actual national park. They included designated trailheads, road markers, and even went so far as to build public restrooms that look unpleasantly familiar to anyone who’s ever used the real deal. The park also has a visitor center with a wooden porch, green railings, tourists milling around outside, and a sign above the entrance reading, “True wanderers are never lost.”.

Industry observers note that it holds far more wildlife than I managed to spot in one visit, too. Rockstar told gaming publication Game Informer that Leonida contains more than 170 animal species, and The Guardian reported that players can identify 62 types of birds using binoculars and record them in a wildlife logbook.

Recent findings suggest that inside Mount Kalaga National Park, I found designated hiking trails dotted with wildflowers and packed with both sporty dog walkers and out-of-breath tourists alike, alongside an elaborate, technical mountain bike trail system. Complete with marked access routes, wooden bridges, and built-out ramps and drops, it looked like a legitimate, and genuinely difficult, trail network, with a time-trial mode built in for players looking to race the course.

I acquired my mountain bike in a way that probably wouldn’t go over well at an actual trailhead; I stole it from a group of unsuspecting riders taking in the view of the lower valley.

After exploring on foot and two wheels and evading a gaggle of angry policemen looking for a bike thief, I paddled a red kayak through a wooded waterway and took a park-service-looking off-road vehicle onto the dirt roads.

Next, I decided to hot-wire a vacant ATV from a trailhead parking lot and set off on a backcountry joyride. From an overlook, I watched rivers wind between tree-lined islands as the sun set, and later, at the top of Mount Kalaga, I looked up at a sky full of stars as the sound of crickets drifted out of the game and into my living room.

What began with a frantic search for the last PlayStation 5 in stock at Target and a virtual armed robbery, ended with a peaceful evening in what might be the most meticulously detailed national park ever created for a video game.
